item.title: Single vs Multi Lane Waiting
item.description:
Introduction

Whenever you step into a bank or a grocery store, you encounter one of two queueing designs:

  1. Multi-Line Queuing ($c \times M/M/1$): Each register or counter has its own dedicated line. Customers pick a line and wait.
  2. Single-Line Queuing ($M/M/c$): A single “serpentine” line feeds into all available counters. The person at the front goes to the next open station.

While multi-line setups might feel faster because individual lines look shorter, single-line systems are mathematically superior in both average wait time and queue stability. Using Markov Chain theory and Queueing Theory, we can prove why pooling capacity eliminates systemic inefficiencies.

System Setup & Assumptions

Consider a facility with $c$ identical servers (e.g., checkout counters), each serving customers at an average rate of $\mu$ (customers per unit time).

Customers arrive at an overall average rate of $\lambda$. We assume standard Markovian properties (Kendall’s Notation $M/M/\dots$):

  • Arrival Process ($M$): Memoryless Poisson process with inter-arrival rate $\lambda$.
  • Service Time ($M$): Memoryless exponential distribution with mean service time $\frac{1}{\mu}$.

To compare both configurations fairly, we set the total traffic intensity (utilization) as:

$$\rho = \frac{\lambda}{c\mu}$$

For the queue to remain stable and not grow infinitely, we require $\rho < 1$.

1. Multi-Line Queuing: $c$ Independent $M/M/1$ Queues

In a multi-line setup, incoming customers split evenly across the $c$ queues (either randomly or by choosing the shortest line upon entry). Assuming an even distribution without queue-jumping (jockeying), each queue behaves as an independent $M/M/1$ model:

  • Arrival rate per line: $\lambda_{\text{line}} = \frac{\lambda}{c}$
  • Service rate per server: $\mu$
  • Traffic intensity per line: $\rho = \frac{\lambda/c}{\mu} = \frac{\lambda}{c\mu}$

Markov Chain State Space for $M/M/1$

For a single $M/M/1$ queue, let $N(t)$ be the number of customers in that specific line at time $t$. The system transitions according to a continuous-time birth-death process:

 ( 0 )  <--λ/c--  ( 1 )  <--λ/c--  ( 2 )  <--λ/c--  ( 3 ) ...
        -- μ -->         -- μ -->         -- μ -->

The expected waiting time in queue $W_q$ for an $M/M/1$ line is given by:

$$W_q^{(M/M/1)} = \frac{\rho}{\mu(1 - \rho)} = \frac{\lambda}{c\mu^2 - \mu\lambda}$$

2. Single-Line Queuing: The $M/M/c$ System

In a single-line system, all arrivals join a central queue served by $c$ channels.

Markov Chain State Space for $M/M/c$

Let $N(t)$ be the total number of customers in the entire system (queue + servers). The state transition rates change depending on how many servers are currently active:

 ( 0 )  <--λ--  ( 1 )  <--λ--  ( 2 ) ... <--λ-- ( c )  <--λ--  ( c+1 ) ...
        --μ-->         --2μ->                  --cμ->          -- cμ ->
  • When $n < c$ customers are present, $n$ servers are working, yielding a total service rate of $n\mu$.
  • When $n \ge c$ customers are present, all $c$ servers are busy, yielding a maximum system service rate of $c\mu$.

Using the steady-state probability of zero customers $P_0$:

$$P_0 = \left[ \sum_{k=0}^{c-1} \frac{(c\rho)^k}{k!} + \frac{(c\rho)^c}{c!(1-\rho)} \right]^{-1}$$

The probability that an arriving customer must wait in line is given by the Erlang-C formula:

$$P_W = C(c, \lambda/\mu) = \frac{\frac{(c\rho)^c}{c!(1-\rho)}}{\sum_{k=0}^{c-1} \frac{(c\rho)^k}{k!} + \frac{(c\rho)^c}{c!(1-\rho)}}$$

The expected waiting time in queue for $M/M/c$ is:

$$W_q^{(M/M/c)} = \frac{P_W}{c\mu - \lambda}$$

Mathematical Proof of Efficiency: The “Idle Server Waste”

Why is $W_q^{(M/M/c)}$ strictly less than $W_q^{(M/M/1)}$? The core difference lies in the state space structure.

In a multi-line system with $c$ separate queues, the system state is represented by a vector $(n_1, n_2, \dots, n_c)$, where $n_i$ is the number of customers in line $i$. Because lines are independent, there exists a non-zero probability of reaching a state where:

$$n_1 > 1 \quad \text{and} \quad n_2 = 0$$

In this state, Server 2 sits completely idle while a customer waits in Line 1. The total processing capacity of the system drops to $(c-1)\mu$, artificially inflating the average wait time across all customers.

In contrast, an $M/M/c$ single-line system guarantees that no server sits idle as long as there is at least one customer waiting in the queue. Service capacity is dynamically pooled, enforcing maximum processing power ($c\mu$) whenever $N \ge c$.

Numerical Example

Consider a system with $c = 2$ servers, each serving $\mu = 1$ customer per minute, and an overall arrival rate of $\lambda = 1.6$ customers per minute ($\rho = 0.8$).

Multi-Line System ($2 \times M/M/1$)

  • Arrival rate per line: $\lambda_{\text{line}} = 0.8$
  • Expected wait time in queue:
$$W_q^{(M/M/1)} = \frac{0.8}{1(1 - 0.8)} = \mathbf{4.0 \text{ minutes}}$$

Single-Line System ($M/M/2$)

  • System arrival rate: $\lambda = 1.6$
  • First, compute $P_0$:
$$P_0 = \left[ 1 + 1.6 + \frac{1.6^2}{2!(1 - 0.8)} \right]^{-1} = \left[ 1 + 1.6 + 6.4 \right]^{-1} = \frac{1}{9} \approx 0.111$$
  • Next, evaluate Erlang-C ($P_W$):
$$P_W = \frac{6.4}{9} \approx 0.711$$
  • Expected wait time in queue:
$$W_q^{(M/M/2)} = \frac{0.711}{2(1) - 1.6} = \frac{0.711}{0.4} = \mathbf{1.78 \text{ minutes}}$$

Result: By merging two independent queues into a single line, the average waiting time drops from 4.0 minutes to 1.78 minutes—a 55.5% reduction in delay with no extra staffing costs.

Summary Comparison

Property Multi-Line ($c \times M/M/1$) Single-Line ($M/M/c$)
Idle Capacity Waste High (Servers idle while other lines wait) Zero (Servers process whenever queue $> 0$)
Wait Time Variance High (Stuck behind slow transactions) Low (A single long task only delays 1 server)
Queue Policy First-Come, First-Served per line Strict First-Come, First-Served overall
Psychological Fairness Low (Perceived unfairness if adjacent lines move faster) High (Guaranteed equity)

Single-line queuing leverages capacity pooling to prevent server idleness, lower expected wait times, and dramatically compress queue variance.

💡
Tip
Key Takeaway: Pooling capacity converts $c$ fragile individual bottlenecks into one resilient service pool. Even when total throughput capacity is identical ($c\mu$), multi-line systems waste server time whenever any line becomes temporarily empty while others are backlogged.

Tweak the arrival rate total_lambda, service rate mu, or number of checkout counters c, then click Run (WASM) to compute the wait time reduction live:

item.title: Installing PyTorch with CUDA & PyG in Conda
item.description:
Setting up PyTorch with GPU acceleration and compiled C++/CUDA extension libraries (like PyTorch Geometric / PyG) often leads to subtle binary mismatch errors. Following this verified sequence ensures complete binary compatibility between PyTorch, the CUDA runtime, and PyG wheels.

1. Create an Isolated Conda Environment

Always start from a fresh environment with a supported Python version (Python 3.10 or 3.11 are currently the most broadly supported across deep learning wheels):

conda create -n torch_cu python=3.11 -y
conda activate torch_cu

2. Install PyTorch with CUDA Wheel Binaries

Upgrade pip within the environment, verify that which python points to the active Conda environment, and install PyTorch with the targeted CUDA index:

conda install pip -y
python -m pip install --upgrade pip

# Install PyTorch, torchvision, and torchaudio with CUDA 12.x / 13.x wheel support
python -m pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121

Note: If your GPU requires CUDA 12.4 or 13.0+, adjust the index URL accordingly (e.g. cu124 or cu130).

3. Verify PyTorch and CUDA Compatibility

Before installing extension libraries, inspect the exact resolved PyTorch version and compiled CUDA tag:

python -c "import torch; print('Torch:', torch.__version__); print('CUDA Runtime:', torch.version.cuda); print('CUDA Available:', torch.cuda.is_available())"

Expected output:

Torch: 2.x.x+cu121
CUDA Runtime: 12.1
CUDA Available: True

4. Install PyTorch Geometric (PyG) and Extension Wheels

Install torch-geometric alongside its optional hardware-accelerated C++ kernels (pyg_lib, torch_scatter, torch_sparse, torch_spline_conv). Match the wheel directory URL to your exact PyTorch version and CUDA tag:

pip install torch-geometric

# Example for PyTorch 2.3.0 with CUDA 12.1 (replace with your matching versions)
pip install pyg_lib torch_scatter torch_sparse torch_spline_conv -f https://data.pyg.org/whl/torch-2.3.0+cu121.html

5. Comprehensive Hardware Verification Script

Run the following one-liner to verify that PyTorch detects your GPU, initializes CUDA context, and loads PyG without errors:

python -c '
import torch
import torch_geometric
import pyg_lib, torch_scatter, torch_sparse

print(f"PyTorch Version:    {torch.__version__}")
print(f"CUDA Available:     {torch.cuda.is_available()}")
if torch.cuda.is_available():
    print(f"Device Count:       {torch.cuda.device_count()}")
    print(f"Primary GPU:        {torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}")
    print(f"VRAM Allocated:     {torch.cuda.memory_allocated(0) / 1024**2:.1f} MB")
print("PyG & C++ Kernels:  Loaded successfully!")
'

If successful, you will see your GPU model name (e.g. NVIDIA GeForce RTX ...) and a confirmation that all C++ kernels loaded cleanly. You can now proceed to install other packages via pip or conda.

item.title: Deploy local AI via Ollama, Open-WebUI and VSCode/VSCodium
item.description:
This guide walks you through installing Ollama on a Linux system, serving it to a strictly local localhost WebUI (ensuring no exposure to the internet), and leveraging your local Large Language Models (LLMs) as an AI Chat Agent and autocomplete engine inside VSCode and/or VSCodium.

Why Run Local AI?

  • No Root / Sudo Required: Runs completely within user space under your home directory.
  • 100% Private & Air-Gapped: Zero external telemetry, no data scraping by third parties, and all inference remains strictly on localhost.
  • Cost Effective: No API subscriptions, token charges, or usage caps.
  • Web Search Extensibility: Open-WebUI can optionally connect to search backends (such as DuckDuckGo / SearXNG) for live Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

Prerequisites & Hardware Considerations

  • Hardware Acceleration: While lightweight quantized models (1B–3B parameters) run comfortably on modern CPUs, responsive interactive coding and 7B+ parameter models perform best on dedicated GPUs with 8 GB+ VRAM (NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, or Apple Silicon unified memory).
  • Scope: This guide focuses on a secure, localhost-only developer setup on Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, Arch, Fedora). Native installers are also available for Windows and macOS.

1. Install Ollama

Create the Directory Structure

First, let’s create a dedicated, isolated folder structure inside your local home directory to keep everything organized.

mkdir -p ~/ollama/{bin,lib,logs,models,webui}
  • bin/: Stores the Ollama executable.
  • lib/: Holds necessary libraries and dependencies.
  • logs/: Keeps tracking and server logs.
  • models/: Stores downloaded LLMs (e.g., Llama, Mistral, Qwen).
  • webui/: Reserved for our frontend interface files.

Download and Move the Binary

Fetch the latest standalone Linux binary directly from Ollama and make it executable:

# Download the latest binary
curl -L https://ollama.com/download/ollama-linux-amd64 -o ~/ollama/bin/ollama

# Make it executable
chmod +x ~/ollama/bin/ollama

Configure Environment Variables

Open your bash configuration file to point your system to these custom directories:

nano ~/.bashrc

Scroll to the bottom of the file and paste the following lines:

export PATH=~/ollama/bin:$PATH
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=~/ollama/lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
export OLLAMA_MODELS=~/ollama/models

Save and exit (Ctrl+X, then Y, then Enter), then reload your terminal profile:

source ~/.bashrc

Start the Ollama Server & Pull a Model

Launch the background server process and download your first programming-focused LLM. In this case, we will use qwen3-coder:30b.

# Start the server in the background
nohup ollama serve > ~/ollama/logs/server.log 2>&1 &

# Pull and run the model
ollama run qwen3-coder:30b

Note: Pulling a 30B model will take some time depending on your internet connection. Once complete, you can test it by typing a prompt directly in your terminal, then type /exit to return to the normal bash prompt.

2. Install Open-WebUI

To enjoy a clean, ChatGPT-like browser interface at http://localhost:8080, we will install Open-WebUI using Python. Open-WebUI is a lightweight, open-source frontend that connects to your local Ollama server. It is heavily extensible and supports all the features you would expect from a modern LLM interface.

Create a Conda Environment (Optional but Recommended)

Using a virtual environment prevents package dependency conflicts with your base system.

conda create --name ollama_webui python=3.11 -y
conda activate ollama_webui
conda install pip -y

Install and Launch Open-WebUI

Install the package via pip:

python -m pip install open-webui

To quickly verify everything works, start the service manually:

open-webui serve

Open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:8080. Create your initial admin account. Since this application runs 100% locally on your machine, your credentials never leave your computer. Test the UI by selecting qwen3-coder:30b from the top dropdown menu and starting a conversation.

3. Automate Startup at Boot

To avoid manually running multiple commands every time you restart your PC, we can automate the process with a lightweight startup script and a cronjob.

Create the Startup Script

nano ~/ollama/start_ollama_webui.sh

Paste the following complete script:

#!/bin/bash

# 1. Load your profile environment variables (for Ollama paths)
source ~/.bashrc

# 2. Start the Ollama server in the background if it isn't running
if ! pkill -0 ollama; then
    nohup ollama serve > ~/ollama/logs/ollama.log 2>&1 &
    sleep 3 # Give it a moment to initialize
fi

# 3. Bind Open WebUI strictly to localhost only and run it
export HOST=127.0.0.1
export PORT=8080

# Initialize Conda for non-interactive shell execution
# (Adjust 'miniforge3', 'miniconda3', or 'anaconda3' path depending on your setup)
eval "$($HOME/miniforge3/bin/conda shell.bash hook)"

conda activate ollama_webui
nohup open-webui serve > ~/ollama/logs/ollama_webui.log 2>&1 &

echo "Ollama and Open-WebUI started successfully!"

Make the script executable:

chmod +x ~/ollama/start_ollama_webui.sh

Register the Cronjob

Open your system’s user crontab configuration:

crontab -e

Hint: If prompted to choose an editor, select nano by typing its corresponding number.

Add this single line at the very bottom of the file:

@reboot ~/ollama/start_ollama_webui.sh

Save and exit. Your system will now spin up both your backend LLM server and frontend UI silently on every boot. You can also trigger it manually anytime by executing bash ~/ollama/start_ollama_webui.sh.

4. Connect Ollama to VSCodium

Standard extensions like GitHub Copilot force you to log into external servers even when trying to hit a local endpoint. To keep things fully local, open, and private, we will use Continue, an outstanding open-source alternative.

Install the Extension

  1. Open VSCodium and navigate to the Extensions tab on the left sidebar (Ctrl+Shift+X).
  2. Search for Continue.
  3. Click Install and select Trust Authors if prompted.

Configure Continue for Advanced Coding

Click the Continue icon in your left sidebar, click the gear/config icon at the bottom of its panel to open config.yaml, and replace its contents with this production-ready setup. Adapt to the models you have downloaded and your hardware capabilities.

name: VSCodium Setup
version: 1.0.0
schema: v1

disableIndexing: false
ignoreRules:
  - "../**"               # Bars checking any directory above the current workspace
  - "**/node_modules/**"
  - "**/.git/**"
  - "**/__pycache__/**"
  - "*.env"
  - "*.vscode"

models:
  # Automatically pulls any model you download via Ollama for Chat/Edit roles
  - name: Ollama Autodetect
    provider: ollama
    model: AUTODETECT
    roles:
      - chat
      - edit
      - apply
    requestOptions:
      timeout: 300 # 5 minute default timeout

  # Fast ghost-text autocomplete (Runs while you type)
  - name: Qwen 2.5 Coder 7B (Autocomplete)
    provider: ollama
    model: qwen2.5-coder:7b
    roles:
      - autocomplete
  # Note: Use qwen2.5-coder:1.5b instead if your hardware experiences lag here.

  # Heavy-lifting configuration for deep thinking / repository restructuring
  - name: "qwen3-coder:30b (deep mode)"
    provider: "ollama"
    model: "qwen3-coder:30b"
    requestOptions:
      timeout: 1200 # 20 minute timeout for massive context processing
    extraBodyProperties:
      keep_alive: 30s # Automatically frees VRAM after 30 seconds of inactivity
      options:

This guide walks you through installing Ollama on a Linux system, serving it to a strictly local localhost WebUI (ensuring no exposure to the internet), and leveraging your local Large Language Models (LLMs) as an AI Chat Agent and autocomplete engine inside VSCode and/or VSCodium.

Why Run Local AI?

  • No Root / Sudo Required: Runs completely within user space under your home directory.
  • 100% Private & Air-Gapped: Zero external telemetry, no data scraping by third parties, and all inference remains strictly on localhost.
  • Cost Effective: No API subscriptions, token charges, or usage caps.
  • Web Search Extensibility: Open-WebUI can optionally connect to search backends (such as DuckDuckGo / SearXNG) for live Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

Prerequisites & Hardware Considerations

  • Hardware Acceleration: While lightweight quantized models (1B–3B parameters) run comfortably on modern CPUs, responsive interactive coding and 7B+ parameter models perform best on dedicated GPUs with 8 GB+ VRAM (NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, or Apple Silicon unified memory).
  • Scope: This guide focuses on a secure, localhost-only developer setup on Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, Arch, Fedora). Native installers are also available for Windows and macOS.

1. Install Ollama

Create the Directory Structure

First, let’s create a dedicated, isolated folder structure inside your local home directory to keep everything organized.

mkdir -p ~/ollama/{bin,lib,logs,models,webui}
  • bin/: Stores the Ollama executable.
  • lib/: Holds necessary libraries and dependencies.
  • logs/: Keeps tracking and server logs.
  • models/: Stores downloaded LLMs (e.g., Llama, Mistral, Qwen).
  • webui/: Reserved for our frontend interface files.

Download and Move the Binary

Fetch the latest standalone Linux binary directly from Ollama and make it executable:

# Download the latest binary
curl -L https://ollama.com/download/ollama-linux-amd64 -o ~/ollama/bin/ollama

# Make it executable
chmod +x ~/ollama/bin/ollama

Open your bash configuration file to point your system to these custom directories:

nano ~/.bashrc

Scroll to the bottom of the file and paste the following lines:

export PATH=~/ollama/bin:$PATH
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=~/ollama/lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
export OLLAMA_MODELS=~/ollama/models

Save and exit (Ctrl+X, then Y, then Enter), then reload your terminal profile:

source ~/.bashrc

Start the Ollama Server & Pull a Model

Launch the background server process and download your first programming-focused LLM. In this case, we will use qwen3-coder:30b.

# Start the server in the background
nohup ollama serve > ~/ollama/logs/server.log 2>&1 &

# Pull and run the model
ollama run qwen3-coder:30b

Note: Pulling a 30B model will take some time depending on your internet connection. Once complete, you can test it by typing a prompt directly in your terminal, then type /exit to return to the normal bash prompt.

2. Install Open-WebUI

To enjoy a clean, ChatGPT-like browser interface at http://localhost:8080, we will install Open-WebUI using Python. Open-WebUI is a lightweight, open-source frontend that connects to your local Ollama server. It is heavily extensible and supports all the features you would expect from a modern LLM interface.

Create a Conda Environment (Optional but Recommended)

Using a virtual environment prevents package dependency conflicts with your base system.

conda create --name ollama_webui python=3.11 -y
conda activate ollama_webui
conda install pip -y

Install and Launch Open-WebUI

Install the package via pip:

python -m pip install open-webui

To quickly verify everything works, start the service manually:

open-webui serve

Open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:8080. Create your initial admin account. Since this application runs 100% locally on your machine, your credentials never leave your computer. Test the UI by selecting qwen3-coder:30b from the top dropdown menu and starting a conversation.

3. Automate Startup at Boot

To avoid manually running multiple commands every time you restart your PC, we can automate the process with a lightweight startup script and a cronjob.

Create the Startup Script

nano ~/ollama/start_ollama_webui.sh

Paste the following complete script:

#!/bin/bash

# 1. Load your profile environment variables (for Ollama paths)
source ~/.bashrc

# 2. Start the Ollama server in the background if it isn't running
if ! pkill -0 ollama; then
    nohup ollama serve > ~/ollama/logs/ollama.log 2>&1 &
    sleep 3 # Give it a moment to initialize
fi

# 3. Bind Open WebUI strictly to localhost only and run it
export HOST=127.0.0.1
export PORT=8080

# Initialize Conda for non-interactive shell execution
# (Adjust 'miniforge3', 'miniconda3', or 'anaconda3' path depending on your setup)
eval "$($HOME/miniforge3/bin/conda shell.bash hook)"

conda activate ollama_webui
nohup open-webui serve > ~/ollama/logs/ollama_webui.log 2>&1 &

echo "Ollama and Open-WebUI started successfully!"

Make the script executable:

chmod +x ~/ollama/start_ollama_webui.sh

Register the Cronjob

Open your system’s user crontab configuration:

crontab -e

Hint: If prompted to choose an editor, select nano by typing its corresponding number.

Add this single line at the very bottom of the file:

@reboot ~/ollama/start_ollama_webui.sh

Save and exit. Your system will now spin up both your backend LLM server and frontend UI silently on every boot. You can also trigger it manually anytime by executing bash ~/ollama/start_ollama_webui.sh.

4. Connect Ollama to VSCodium

Standard extensions like GitHub Copilot force you to log into external servers even when trying to hit a local endpoint. To keep things fully local, open, and private, we will use Continue, an outstanding open-source alternative.

Install the Extension

  1. Open VSCodium and navigate to the Extensions tab on the left sidebar (Ctrl+Shift+X).
  2. Search for Continue.
  3. Click Install and select Trust Authors if prompted.

  - "../**"               # Bars checking any directory above the current workspace
  - "**/node_modules/**"

item.title: Install Custom Applications on Linux
item.description:
Overview

When using Linux machines where you lack root privileges (sudo), you can still install applications locally. This guide covers how to set up standalone binaries (like VS Code, Obsidian, or custom tools) and integrate them into your desktop environment’s app launcher using .desktop files.

Step-by-Step Installation

1. Download and Prepare

Download the executable or compressed archive (.tar.gz, .zip, .AppImage) for your application. If it’s a folder, move it to a dedicated local bin directory.

Example Path:

/home_local/username/bin/myapp/

but you can of course use another directory as well.

2. Make the application executable

  1. Find the main binary executable file in the folder.

    ls /home_local/username/bin/myapp

  2. Use chmod to grant execution permissions to it

    Let’s say we found the executable to be named myapp as well. If you downloaded a .AppImage, use this file instead.

    chmod +x /home_local/username/bin/myapp/myapp

3. Add to System PATH (Optional)

If you want to run the application from any terminal by just typing its name, you can add it to your .bashrc.

Note: On some systems, the bin folder might already be in your PATH.

  1. Open your bash configuration: 
    nano ~/.bashrc
  2. Add this line at the end: 
    export PATH="/home_local/username/bin/myapp:$PATH"
  3. Apply changes: 
    source ~/.bashrc

4. Create a Desktop Entry

To make the application appear in your app launcher (Super key / Start menu), create a .desktop file.

  1. Create the file:

    nano ~/.local/share/applications/myapp.desktop

  2. Paste the following template and adjust the paths:

    [Desktop Entry]
Version=1.0
Type=Application
Name=My Application
Comment=A short description of the app
Exec=/net/rmc-lx0181/home_local/fuer_jk/bin/myapp/executablefile
Icon=/net/rmc-lx0181/home_local/fuer_jk/bin/myapp/icon.png
Terminal=false
Categories=Utility;Application;

5. Finalize and Refresh

Make the desktop entry itself executable and update the desktop database.

chmod +x ~/.local/share/applications/myapp.desktop
update-desktop-database ~/.local/share/applications

6. Search for your App

Press the Super key (Windows key) and search for your application name.

Troubleshooting Tips

  • Binary not found: Ensure the Exec path is absolute and points to the actual file, not its containing folder.
  • Icon not showing: Ensure the Icon path points to a valid .png or .svg file.
  • Validation: Run desktop-file-validate ~/.local/share/applications/myapp.desktop to check for syntax errors.

item.title: Git & GitHub
item.description:
“Git is a distributed version control software system that is capable of managing versions of source code or data. It is often used to control source code by programmers who are developing software collaboratively.” [Wikipedia as of 2025-05-30]

I. Setup & Configuration

1. Install Git

(Test if installed: git --version)

Windows

winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget

macOS

brew install git

Linux

# Debian, Ubuntu, Raspberry Pi OS
sudo apt install git

# Arch Linux
sudo pacman -S git

# Fedora
sudo dnf install git

# NixOS / Nix
nix-env -iA nixpkgs.git

2. Install GitHub CLI (gh)

Essential for PRs and repo management from the terminal.

Windows: winget install --id GitHub.cli

macOS: brew install gh

Linux: sudo apt install gh or sudo pacman -S github-cli

Authenticate:

gh auth login

3. Basic Config

Set your identity for all local repositories:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "developer@example.com"

Note: Remove --global to use a different identity for just the current folder.

If using a credential manager, clear stored credentials if needed:

git credential-cache exit

4. SSH Authentication (Optional)

Recommended for secure, passwordless access.

  1. Create Key: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "jokobus@example.com"
  2. Path: Press Enter for default or specify a path (e.g., ~/.ssh/id_ed25519).
  3. Add to Agent: ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  4. Add to GitHub: Copy the public key (id_ed25519.pub) content to GitHub Settings -> SSH and GPG keys.
  5. Test: ssh -T git@github.com
  6. Switch Remote: git remote set-url origin git@github.com:user/repo.git

II. Local Git Basics

Init

Initiate an empty git repository (in your current working directory, so cd/mkdir first). Afterwards git can track file/folder changes (add/remove/edit) in that directory.

git init

Status & Diff

  • git status: See what changes are staged/unstaged.
  • git diff: See actual changes in unstaged files.
  • git diff --staged: See changes waiting to be committed.

Stage

Add (stage) changes to the next commit.

git add <file>  # Stage a specific file
git add .       # Stage all changes in current directory
git add -A      # Stage all changes in the entire repository (including deletions)

Commit

git commit -m "Some message"
git commit -a -m "Some message" # -a commits all changes directly, skipping stage (for small changes, not recommended), or use -am

Log & Help

Log:

  • git log: Detailed history.
  • git log --oneline: Compact history.
  • git log --oneline --graph --all: Visual branch structure.
  • git log -5: Show last five commits

Tip: Use the arrow keys to navigate up/down and type :q for quit.

Help:

  • git <command> --help: Get help for a specific command.
  • git help --all: List all available commands.

Branches

Create a branch (~copy) of the main branch, edit your branch and merge it with the main branch.

git branch mybranch      # create new branch called mybranch
git branch                      # verify in which branch you are (* main)
git checkout mybranch    # therefore switch to new branch

# alternative: create and move to new branch in one line
git checkout -b mybranch

After making changes, add, commit and merge.

git add -A
git commit -m "Some message"    # Commit to mybranch
git checkout main             	# Switch back to main
git merge mybranch
git branch -d mybranch   # Delete temporary branch after successful merge

If the merge fails due to a conflict, edit the file and commit again.

III. GitHub Integration

Important: Always stay up to date (git pull origin main)! Working on outdated versions makes merging a nightmare.

1. Connect to Remote

  • Clone existing repo: 
    git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
# OR via SSH (preferred, if you have already created an SSH keypair)
git clone git@github.com:user/repo.git
  • Add remote to local repo: 
    git remote add origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
git push -u origin main

2. Useful Commands

  • git fetch origin: Download latest version from GitHub (no merge).
  • git pull origin: Download and merge (Fetch + Merge).
  • git status: Show state of current repository.
  • git branch -a: Show all local and remote branches.
  • git branch -d <name>: Delete a merged branch.
  • git branch -D <name>: Force delete an unmerged branch.
  • git diff origin/main: Show differences between current branch and main.
  • git remote -v: List connected remotes (URL).
  • git remote show origin: Detailed remote information.

3. Disconnect from a GitHub Repository

git remote remove origin
git remote -v  # If nothing printed, you are disconnected.

IV. Guided Workflows

1. Simple Local Workflow

Use this for solo projects or small fixes. Tip: use branches for no matter how small the change is, as this is only a small extra overhead but an excellent practice and avoids many issues (or saves your life) when anything goes wrong.

  1. Keep updated and in sync with main (very important!): 
    git pull origin main
  2. Create new branch: 
    git branch mybranch
git checkout mybranch
    or as a one-liner: 
    git checkout -b mybranch
  3. Make changes: In that branch, do whatever changes and commit them.
  4. Merge back to main: 
    git checkout main
git pull origin main
git merge mybranch
    If you get a Merge Conflict -> resolve manually and decide whether to keep HEAD/main or edits from mybranch. 
    git push origin main
  5. Post-merge:
    • Option A: Delete branch 
      git branch -d mybranch
    • Option B: Reuse branch 
      git checkout mybranch
git pull origin main
git merge main
      (After merging mybranch into main, merge main back into mybranch to keep it updated).
  6. Start again from step 1 for the next feature.

2. Workflow with GitHub / Pull Requests (PRs)

via GitHub Website

  1. Create, checkout and commit to a new branch.
  2. Push branch: Push your branch to GitHub. 
    git push origin mybranch
  3. Create PR: Open the repo on GitHub.com and create a new PR from your branch.
  4. Review and Merge: Once reviewed, merge the PR on GitHub.
    • If changes are requested (from a coworker, repo-maintainer, etc.), keep working on that branch and commit the changes to it: the PR is updated automatically.
    • Wait until the PR is merged, before you delete the branch.
  5. Clean up: GitHub has a “Delete branch” button once the PR is closed.
  6. Start again from step 1.

Method B: Via Terminal (GitHub CLI gh)

  1. Pull latest changes: 
    git pull origin main
  2. Create new feature branch: 
    git checkout -b mybranch
  3. Work: Make changes and commit locally.
  4. Push & PR: Push branch and create the PR from the terminal: 
    git push -u origin mybranch
gh pr create --base main
    (Follow the interactive terminal prompts for Title/Body, or use --title "..." --body "..." flags).
  5. Iterate: If changes are requested, keep working locally and push. The PR updates automatically.
  6. Merge: Once approved, merge from the terminal: bash gh pr merge --merge --delete-branch
  7. Start again from step 1.

V. Utilities & Fixing Mistakes

Saving Work (Stash)

Use when you need to switch branches quickly but aren’t ready to commit.

git stash save "working on feature x" 	# Save changes
git stash list                        	# View saved work
git stash pop                         	# Bring changes back
git stash pop stash@{X}					# specifying which stash to pop (replace X)

Fixing Mistakes

  • Undo file change: git checkout -- <filename> (Discard local changes).
  • Amend: git commit --amend -m "New message" (Modify last commit message).
  • Revert: git revert HEAD (Undoes last commit safely via a new “undo” commit).
  • Reset: git reset <hash> (Moves back to a previous commit, discarding newer work). Caution: Destructive!
  • Emergency Rescue: git reflog (Shows history of all actions; find “lost” commits here).

Ignoring Files (.gitignore)

Create a .gitignore file in your repository root to skip logs or private files:

# Ignore all .log files except main.log
*.log
!main.log

# Ignore a specific directory
temp/

Note: Use .git/info/exclude for local-only ignores.

Re-evaluating .gitignore

If you added files to .gitignore that are already being tracked, you must untrack them to enforce the rules:

  1. Remove cached files:
git rm -r --cached .
  1. Re-add everything:
git add .
  1. Commit changes:
git commit -m "Untrack ignored files and apply .gitignore"

Git push branch delete to github

To delete the branch on GitHub (the remote repository), you need to push a delete command to it.

You can do this by running the following command in your terminal:

git push origin --delete mybranch

Replace mybranch with the exact name of the branch you just deleted locally.

Alternative Short Command

If you prefer a shorter shortcut, you can use a colon (:) before the branch name, which tells Git to push “nothing” into the remote branch:

git push origin :mybranch

Pro-Tip: Clean up your references

Even after deleting the branch on GitHub, your local Git history might still “remember” that the remote branch used to exist. To clean up those outdated references, run:

git fetch origin --prune

“Git is a distributed version control software system that is capable of managing versions of source code or data. It is often used to control source code by programmers who are developing software collaboratively.” [Wikipedia as of 2025-05-30]

I. Setup & Configuration

1. Install Git

(Test if installed: git --version)

Windows

winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget

macOS

brew install git

Linux

# Debian, Ubuntu, Raspberry Pi OS
sudo apt install git

# Arch Linux
sudo pacman -S git

# Fedora
sudo dnf install git

# NixOS / Nix
nix-env -iA nixpkgs.git

2. Install GitHub CLI (gh)

Essential for PRs and repo management from the terminal.

Windows: winget install --id GitHub.cli

macOS: brew install gh

Linux: sudo apt install gh or sudo pacman -S github-cli

Authenticate:

gh auth login

3. Basic Config

Set your identity for all local repositories:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "developer@example.com"

Note: Remove --global to use a different identity for just the current folder.

If using a credential manager, clear stored credentials if needed:

git credential-cache exit

4. SSH Authentication (Optional)

Recommended for secure, passwordless access.

  1. Create Key: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "jokobus@example.com"
  2. Path: Press Enter for default or specify a path (e.g., ~/.ssh/id_ed25519).
  3. Add to Agent: ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  4. Add to GitHub: Copy the public key (id_ed25519.pub) content to GitHub Settings -> SSH and GPG keys.
  5. Test: ssh -T git@github.com
  6. Switch Remote: git remote set-url origin git@github.com:user/repo.git

II. Local Git Basics

Init

Initiate an empty git repository (in your current working directory, so cd/mkdir first). Afterwards git can track file/folder changes (add/remove/edit) in that directory.

git init

Status & Diff

  • git status: See what changes are staged/unstaged.
  • git diff: See actual changes in unstaged files.
  • git diff --staged: See changes waiting to be committed.

Stage

Add (stage) changes to the next commit.

git add <file>  # Stage a specific file
git add .       # Stage all changes in current directory
git add -A      # Stage all changes in the entire repository (including deletions)

Commit

git commit -m "Some message"
git commit -a -m "Some message" # -a commits all changes directly, skipping stage (for small changes, not recommended), or use -am

Log & Help

Log:

  • git log: Detailed history.
  • git log --oneline: Compact history.
  • git log --oneline --graph --all: Visual branch structure.
  • git log -5: Show last five commits

Tip: Use the arrow keys to navigate up/down and type :q for quit.

Help:

  • git <command> --help: Get help for a specific command.
  • git help --all: List all available commands.

Branches

Create a branch (~copy) of the main branch, edit your branch and merge it with the main branch.

git branch mybranch      # create new branch called mybranch
git branch                      # verify in which branch you are (* main)
git checkout mybranch    # therefore switch to new branch

# alternative: create and move to new branch in one line
git checkout -b mybranch

After making changes, add, commit and merge.

git add -A
git commit -m "Some message"    # Commit to mybranch
git checkout main             	# Switch back to main
git merge mybranch
git branch -d mybranch   # Delete temporary branch after successful merge

If the merge fails due to a conflict, edit the file and commit again.

III. GitHub Integration

Important: Always stay up to date (git pull origin main)! Working on outdated versions makes merging a nightmare.

1. Connect to Remote

  • Clone existing repo: 
    git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
# OR via SSH (preferred, if you have already created an SSH keypair)
git clone git@github.com:user/repo.git
  • Add remote to local repo: 
    git remote add origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
git push -u origin main

2. Useful Commands

  • git fetch origin: Download latest version from GitHub (no merge).
  • git pull origin: Download and merge (Fetch + Merge).
  • git status: Show state of current repository.
  • git branch -a: Show all local and remote branches.
  • git branch -d <name>: Delete a merged branch.
  • git branch -D <name>: Force delete an unmerged branch.
  • git diff origin/main: Show differences between current branch and main.
  • git remote -v: List connected remotes (URL).
  • git remote show origin: Detailed remote information.

3. Disconnect from a GitHub Repository

git remote remove origin
git remote -v  # If nothing printed, you are disconnected.

IV. Guided Workflows

1. Simple Local Workflow

Use this for solo projects or small fixes. Tip: use branches for no matter how small the change is, as this is only a small extra overhead but an excellent practice and avoids many issues (or saves your life) when anything goes wrong.

  1. Keep updated and in sync with main (very important!): 
    git pull origin main
  2. Create new branch: 
    git branch mybranch
git checkout mybranch
    or as a one-liner: 
    git checkout -b mybranch
  3. Make changes: In that branch, do whatever changes and commit them.
  4. Merge back to main: 
    git checkout main
git pull origin main
git merge mybranch
    If you get a Merge Conflict -> resolve manually and decide whether to keep HEAD/main or edits from mybranch. 
    git push origin main
  5. Post-merge:
    • Option A: Delete branch 
      git branch -d mybranch
    • Option B: Reuse branch 
      git checkout mybranch
git pull origin main
git merge main
      (After merging mybranch into main, merge main back into mybranch to keep it updated).
  6. Start again from step 1 for the next feature.

2. Workflow with GitHub / Pull Requests (PRs)

via GitHub Website

  1. Create, checkout and commit to a new branch.
  2. Push branch: Push your branch to GitHub. 
    git push origin mybranch
  3. Create PR: Open the repo on GitHub.com and create a new PR from your branch.
  4. Review and Merge: Once reviewed, merge the PR on GitHub.
    • If changes are requested (from a coworker, repo-maintainer, etc.), keep working on that branch and commit the changes to it: the PR is updated automatically.

  5. Clean up: GitHub has a “Delete branch” button once the PR is closed.
  6. Start again from step 1.

  1. Pull latest changes:

  2. Create new feature branch: 
    git checkout -b mybranch
  3. Work: Make changes and commit locally.
  4. Push & PR: Push branch and create the PR from the terminal:

  5. Iterate: If changes are requested, keep working locally and push. The PR updates automatically.
  6. Merge: Once approved, merge from the terminal: bash gh pr merge --merge --delete-branch

  1. Re-add everything:

git push origin --delete mybranch

git tag archive/mybranch mybranch
  1. Push the tag to GitHub
git push origin archive/mybranch

  1. Delete locally
git branch -d mybranch
  1. Delete from GitHub
git push origin --delete mybranch

item.title: Avoid Python Package Import-Errors in VSCodium or VSCode
item.description:
If you are working with Conda environments, you might notice that VSCodium or VS Code shows “import not found” errors (red squiggly lines) even though your code runs perfectly fine in the terminal.

This happens because the IDE’s Python extension doesn’t automatically know which Conda environment to use for its background linting and IntelliSense. By explicitly setting the interpreter path, you tell the IDE exactly where to look for your installed packages.

How to fix it

Option A) Set default interpreter

In your project root, create a .vscode folder and add a settings.json file inside it. Paste the following configuration, replacing the path with the location of your specific environment’s conda python executable:

{
  "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "/Users/username/miniconda3/envs/my-env-name/bin/python"
}

Option B) Ignore all missing imports

If you don’t want to specify an interpreter and simply want to hide the error messages, you can add this to your settings.json instead:

{
  "python.analysis.diagnosticSeverityOverrides": {
    "reportMissingImports": "none"
  }
}

This tells Pylance/Pyright (the language servers) to stop reporting missing imports as errors, though it won’t help with autocompletion.

item.title: Tune VSCodium for Python
item.description:
VSCodium is the privacy-focused, open-source binary release of VS Code, free of Microsoft telemetry.

However, out of the box, VSCodium requires a couple of extension and configuration tweaks to enable seamless autocomplete, syntax highlighting, and hover documentation for Python. Follow these two simple steps to optimize your setup:

1. Install Extensions

Install the

  • Python and
  • Pyright (by ms-pyright)

Extensions via the Extensions Store at the left, vertical bar in VSCodium.

2. Tweak your settings.json

In the search bar enter: > settings.json. Choose the User Settings.json and paste:

{
  "editor.hover.enabled": true,
  "editor.hover.delay": 150,
  "editor.parameterHints.enabled": true,
  "editor.suggestOnTriggerCharacters": true,
  "editor.bracketPairs.enabled": true,
  "editor.guides.bracketPairs": "active",
  "editor.suggest.preview": true,
  "editor.suggest.showDetails": true,
  "python.analysis.typeCheckingMode": "basic"
}

item.title: Ergonomic Typing with Neo Layout (Bone Variant)
item.description:
This is a concise guide to the essentials of the Neo Keyboard Layout variant Bone for faster, healthier typing and streamlined mathematical notation.

Windows

To use it on Windows follow these steps.

Install

  • Copy the kbdbone.dll file in System32 to C:\Windows\System32 and the one in SysWOW64 to C:\Windows\SysWOW64 respectively. Grant access rights. (On 64-bit Windows you have to copy it with a 64-bit Programm, best by the Windows Explorer)

  • Execute the kbdneo_win10_install.reg file, which will add the layout to the registry for you. Again, grant access.

  • Reboot your system

  • In System Settings under Time&Language/Language choose the System Language and choose Bone as your keyboard layout.

  • At each boot: execute reneo.exe (e.g. via Tasksheduler)

Uninstall

The uninstallation is best to be performed in reversed order of the installation

  • Stop reneo.exe

  • In the System Settings, remove the layout from the list

  • Execute the Registry uninstall file kbd_win10_uninstall.reg

  • Delete both kbdneo.dll files from C:\Windows\System32 and _C:\Windows\SysWOW64_s

  • Reboot your computer

Linux

In most Distro’s you can choose Neolayout Bone in your System Settings.

If not (or if it get’s reset at every reboot) you can use the following command:

setxkbmap -layout de -variant bone

or set it back to the normal german

setxkbmap -layout de

I found that it is most convenient to add aliases to my bashrc

nano ~/.bashrc

add the lines (doesn’t matter where, e.g. put it in the first lines)

alias setbone=setxkbmap -layout de -variant bone
alias lfshgjf=setxkbmap -layout de -variant bone
alias setde=setxkbmap -layout de
alias lfswf=setxkbmap -layout de

Finally source the bashrc

source ~/.bashrc

Learn the Layout

Well, the beginning will be tough, but definitely worth it.

For the start, I recommend tipp10 which has the option to learn bone in the online-version (but not in the desktop version). That is definitely a good start for the first few days, where you have to look up every second character.

Afterwards you can set the keymapping of the first layer as your Desktop background image, so you can always look characters up.

Good luck and stay with it!

item.title: OOBE
item.description:
What is OOBE?

OOBE is the Windows Out of Box Experience, that you have to click through after a fresh installation of Windows on your Computer. There you can set the system language, keyboard layout, connect to the internet and

Problem 1: Windows wants to force you to use a Microsoft Account

Microsoft wants you to use a Microsoft Account that is connected to their Cloud - to use all the amazing online Microsoft Features (and conveniently collect your data. Mpf). But instead of adding a Button “Use local account instead” they lay stones in your path. What a surprise! Solution 1 helps

Problem 2: You don’t have a internet connection at hand

If you don’t have an Internet connection at hand, Solution 1 works for you as well. Note: Now you have to create a Local Account, a Microsoft Account is not possible without an Internet connection. (But you can always switch/convert to a Microsoft Account in the account settings once you have finished setting Windows up - for whatever reason you should like to do that. )

Solution 1 & 2: Install Windows with a Local Account

Once booted a screen will show up to ask you to connect to your Wifi.

Instead, press Ctrl + F10 (or Fn + Ctrl + F10 if Fn always needs to be pressed for the function keys).

This will showm up a Command Prompt window. There type:

oobe \bypassnro

The computer will restart automatically. Afterwards, there will be a button Continue with limited setup in the step where you should setup the wifi. Click it and continue with setting up your Local Account.

Problem 3: Bypass OOBE temporarily

If you want to setup the computer with a Local Account, follow solution 1. This guide is for a different use case: You want to sell / give away your computer. You have Windows freshly installed and want to enter it (temporarily) to install drivers, updates or just see that everything is working fine. But you want that the person who gets the computer enters the OOBE and can setup everything else for themselve - with a fresh Feeling and no leftover config / wifi connection passwords from your side. In that case you can bypass OOBE.

Solution 3: Bypass OOBE temporarily

Method 1 - Key combination

Press the key combination Ctrl+Shift+F3. That should normally be the easiest way.

Note: Sometimes the Fn key is locked in the Bios Settings, then you would have to press Ctrl+Fn+Shift+F3.

Method 2

On the first OOBE screen, press Ctrl+F10 (or Ctrl+Fn+F10)

This will show up a Command Prompt window. There type:

cd \Windows\System32\oobe
msobe.exe /bypass

Restart the computer

shutdown /r /t

After the reboot, Windows should directly take you to the login screen.

Method 3 - Registry Entry

You can also try to set a OOBE entry in the Windows Registry.

  1. Press Shift+F10 to open the command prompt during the Windows setup.

Add a registry dword

reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Setup" /v "OOBEComplete" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

Restart your computer with

shutdown /r /t 0

On the next boot Windows should skip OOBE and log you in as a temporary administrator.

After you’re done, open Command Prompt (e.g. via the Startmenu) and execute

reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Setup" /v "OOBEComplete" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

or delete the key entirely

reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Setup" /v "OOBEComplete" /f

Restart the computer and you should be directly taken back to the OOBE.

item.title: PyTorch Essentials: Tensors, Datasets & Deep Learning Basics
item.description:
PyTorch has established itself as the leading research framework for deep learning, offering dynamic computation graphs, seamless GPU acceleration, and an intuitive, Pythonic API.

PyTorch vs. TensorFlow vs. Scikit-Learn

Choosing the right machine learning tool depends on your application scope:

Framework Primary Strengths Ideal Use Case
Scikit-Learn Classical tabular algorithms, fast prototyping, shallow ML Regression, Random Forests, SVMs, clustering, data preprocessing
PyTorch Dynamic graphs (Eager execution), cutting-edge AI research, flexible debugging Deep Learning, Computer Vision, Transformers / LLMs, GNNs
TensorFlow / Keras Static graph compilation, high-throughput deployment Enterprise mobile (TFLite) and distributed server production

Environment Setup & Installation

It is recommended to run PyTorch in an isolated Conda environment. See the companion Conda Essentials Guide or Installing PyTorch with CUDA in Conda.

# Create environment
conda create -n pytorch_env python=3.11 -y
conda activate pytorch_env

# Install PyTorch with CPU or CUDA support
conda install pytorch torchvision torchaudio -c pytorch

Core Imports

import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from torchvision import datasets
from torchvision.transforms import ToTensor

1. What is a Tensor?

Mathematically, a tensor is an algebraic entity describing multilinear relationships over vector spaces. In computer science and deep learning:

  • A 0-D Tensor is a scalar (e.g. $s = 42$).
  • A 1-D Tensor is a vector (e.g. $v = [1, 2, 3]$).
  • A 2-D Tensor is a matrix with rows and columns (e.g. a grayscale image or weight matrix).
  • A 3-D+ Tensor represents higher-dimensional multidimensional arrays (e.g. batch size $\times$ color channels $\times$ height $\times$ width for video/images).

Hands-on Tensor Operations

The script below demonstrates tensor creation, shapes, datatypes, device placement, and NumPy interoperability:

📄 Tensors.py - Basic Tensor Operations
python 
import torch
import numpy as np

# Initialize a Tensor
## Directly from data
data = [[1,2], [3,4]]
x_data = torch.tensor(data)
print(f"From Data: \n{x_data} \n")
## From another NumPy Array
np_array = np.array(data)
x_np = torch.from_numpy(np_array)
print(f"From NumPy: \n{x_np} \n")
## From another tensor
x_ones = torch.ones_like(x_data)
print(f"Ones Tensor: \n{x_ones} \n")
x_rand = torch.rand_like(x_data, dtype=torch.float)
print(f"Random Tensor: \n{x_rand} \n")
## Create tensor with specific shape
shape = (2,3,)
rand_tensor = torch.rand(shape)
ones_tensor = torch.ones(shape)
zeros_tensor = torch.zeros(shape)
print(f"Random 2x3 Tensor: \n{rand_tensor} \n")
print(f"Ones 2x3 Tensor: \n{ones_tensor} \n")

This post is my personal SQL Cheat Sheet, based on the SQL tutorial by W3Schools.

tl;dr SQL let’s you access and manipulate databases.

Why SQL

SQL can execute queries, retrieve data, insert records, update records, delete record to/from a database as well as create/delete a database, create/delete tables in a database, create views and stored procedures in a database and finally set permissions on tables, procedures and views.

Many database programs build on SQL, but add some (proprietary) functionalities.

If you want to embedd database information via SQL on a website you use a database program such as MySQL. Besides you will need a server-side scripting language (PHP) and HTML and CSS for the frontend.

Basics

  • Column = A Feature or observation criteria
  • Row = A Record or observation

Tipp: SQL keywords are not case sensitive

SELECT column1, column2 FROM mytable WHERE condition; 
SELECT * FROM mytable;
select column1, column2 from mytable;

Some of the most important SQL commands

Command Description
SELECT extracts data from a database
UPDATE updates data in a database
DELETE deletes data from a database
INSERT INTO inserts new data into a database
CREATE DATABASE creates a new database
ALTER DATABASE modifies a database
CREATE TABLE cretes a new table
ALTER TABLE modifies a table
DROP TABLE deletes a table
CREATE INDEX creates an index (search key)
DROP INDEX deletes an index

SELECT DISCTINCT

SELECT DISTINCT returns only distinct (non-duplicate) values

SELECT DISTINCT column1 FROM mytable;

You can combine it with the COUNT argument, to count how many distinct entries are there, e.g. in the column Country.

SELECT COUNT (DISTINCT Country) FROM mytable;

ORDER BY

Use the ORDER BY statement to order the order of the rows, e.g. py ascending price.

SELECT column1, column2 FROM mytable ORDER BY column1, column2 ASC|DESC;
SELECT ProductName, Price FROM mytable WHERE Price>=50 ORDER BY Price DESC, ProductName ASC;

WHERE

Appending WHERE you can filter the returned entities. E.g. the following example only returns records where the Country feature is Germany. (Of course the table has to have columns called ‘Country’ and ‘Revenue’. ) Use single quotes for Text / “Strings”.

SELECT * FROM mytable WHERE Country='Germany';
SELECT * FROM mytable WHERE Revenue > 100000;

As in other programming languages, you can use

Operator Description
= equal
> greater than
< less than
>= greater than or equal
<= less than or equal
<> not equal
!= not equal (in some SQL versions)
BETWEEN between a certain range
LIKE search for a pattern
IN to specify multiple possible values for a column

AND, OR, NOT operator

The WHERE clause can contain one or multiple AND, OR and NOT operators. AND and OR are rather self explaining. NOT is used with other operators to invert their result. You can combine multiple operators and use brackets for semantics.

SELECT column1, column2, FROM mytable WHERE condition1 AND (condition2 OR condition3) AND NOT condition4;
SELECT * FROM mytable WHERE Country='Germany' AND Revenue > 1000000;

Some Examples: First, select all entries from countries that start with G (Gambia, Germany, Greece, etc.) or F (Finnland, France, Fidji, etc.) and where the revenue is greater than 100.

SELECT * FROM mytable WHERE Revenue > 100 AND Country LIKE 'G%' OR Country LIKE 'F%'; 
SELECT * FROM mytable WHERE Country IN ('Germany', 'France');

Example: All entrise with a revenue that is not between specific boundaries shall be returned.

SELECT * FROM mytable WHERE Revenue NOT BETWEEN 100 AND 1000;

INSERT INTO

INSERT INTO is used to insert new records in a table. There are two different ways to write it:

  • By using the first command you can specify only specific columns, the rest is left blank (null value). 
    INSERT INTO mytable (column1, column2, column3) VALUES (value1, value2, value3);
  • And with this command you can enter multiple lines (here it’s three) with one call.

item.title: Conda Essentials: Complete Guide & Cheat Sheet
item.description:
Why Conda?

Conda is an open-source package management and environment management system designed for scientific computing, machine learning, and multi-language development (Python, R, C/C++, etc.).

Key advantages of Conda include:

  • Isolated Environments: Every project maintains its own isolated dependency sandbox, preventing version conflicts between libraries (e.g. PyTorch 2.x vs TensorFlow 2.x).
  • Binary Non-Python Dependencies: Unlike pip, which primarily manages Python wheels and packages, Conda can install compiled system libraries (such as CUDA runtimes, cuDNN, OpenBLAS, Graphviz, and HDF5) directly into your environment without requiring root/sudo privileges.
  • Cross-Platform Consistency: Ensures identical dependency resolution across Linux, macOS, and Windows.

Installation: Miniforge vs. Anaconda

While full Anaconda includes a large bundle of pre-installed GUI tools and packages, the recommended modern standard is Miniforge. Miniforge is a minimalist, community-driven installer pre-configured with conda-forge as the default channel (avoiding commercial licensing restrictions of Anaconda’s default channel).

Linux / macOS

Download and run the Miniforge installation script:

# Download installer script
wget https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh

# Run installer (follow prompts, default path ~/.miniforge3 is recommended)
bash Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh

Restart your terminal or reload your shell profile (source ~/.bashrc or source ~/.zshrc).

Windows

Download the executable installer Miniforge3-Windows-x86_64.exe from the conda-forge releases and run the setup wizard.

Verify Installation

conda --version
conda info

Custom Configuration (.condarc)

Conda can be customized globally (~/.condarc) or per-project. For example, to specify custom directory paths for environments and downloaded packages:

# ~/.condarc
envs_dirs:
  - ~/miniconda3/envs
  - /data/shared/conda/envs

pkgs_dirs:
  - ~/miniconda3/pkgs
  - /data/shared/conda/pkgs

channels:
  - conda-forge

To inspect your active runtime configuration:

conda config --show

Managing Environments

1. Create a New Environment

Always specify a project name and desired Python version when creating an environment:

# Create environment with a specific Python version
conda create --name ml_project python=3.11

# Create environment with initial packages
conda create --name cv_project python=3.10 numpy opencv matplotlib

Version Pinning Reference

Constraint Type Syntax Matches
Fuzzy Match python=3.11 Any 3.11.x release (e.g., 3.11.9)
Exact Pin python==3.11.8 Strictly version 3.11.8
Comparison python>=3.10 3.10 or newer
Range (AND) "python>=3.10,<3.12" 3.10.x and 3.11.x, but excluding 3.12
OR `“python=3.10 3.11”`

2. Activate and Deactivate

When an environment is activated, Conda prepends its binary folder to your system PATH:

# Activate target environment
conda activate ml_project

# Terminal prompt reflects the active environment:
# (ml_project) user@workstation:~$

# Deactivate back to base
conda deactivate

Tip: If you prefer your terminal not to automatically activate the base environment on launch, run:

conda config --set auto_activate_base false

3. List Environments

conda env list
# or
conda info --envs

The active environment is indicated with an asterisk (*).

4. Clone and Rename Environments

To duplicate an existing environment:

conda create --name ml_backup --clone ml_project

To rename an environment (Conda 4.14+):

conda rename --name old_name new_name

5. Export and Recreate (Reproducibility)

To share your exact environment state with colleagues or CI/CD pipelines:

# Export environment definition to YAML
conda env export --no-builds > environment.yml

# Recreate environment from YAML
conda env create -f environment.yml

6. Delete an Environment

conda env remove --name ml_backup

Managing Packages

1. Install and Search

# Install a package from conda-forge
conda install pytorch torchvision torchaudio -c pytorch -c nvidia

# Search for available package versions
conda search scikit-learn

2. Update and Remove

# Update a single package
conda update numpy

# Update all packages in the active environment
conda update --all

# Remove a package and its orphaned dependencies
conda remove scipy

3. List Installed Packages

conda list

Essential Cheat Sheet

# Environment Lifecycle
conda create -n <name> python=3.11    # Create new environment
conda activate <name>                 # Activate environment
conda deactivate                      # Exit environment
conda env list                        # Show all environments
conda env remove -n <name>            # Delete environment

# Reproducibility
conda env export --no-builds > env.yml # Export to portable YAML
conda env create -f env.yml           # Recreate from YAML

# Packages
conda install <pkg>                   # Install package
conda update <pkg>                    # Update package
conda remove <pkg>                    # Remove package
conda list                            # List installed packages

item.title: Custom Anki Card
item.description:
Today, I came across my old notes from German class and decided to practice stylistic devices (dt. “Stilmittel”) again. To optimize retention, I built a custom Anki card template utilizing three fields: Name, Definition, and Example. This guide demonstrates how to configure multi-field templates in Anki with automatic cross-learning:

  1. Given Name $\rightarrow$ recall Definition and Example
  2. Given Definition $\rightarrow$ recall Name and Example
  3. Given Example $\rightarrow$ recall Name and Definition

1. Create Template

  1. Go to Tools>Manage Note Types (Ctrl+Shift+N)
  2. Click Add
  3. Choose Add:Basic (and reversed card)
  4. Name it something like Cross Learning (Name, Definition, Example)
  5. Select the newly created Note Type in the list (scroll down)
  6. Click Fields
  7. Rename and Add, so that you have 1:Name, 2:Definition, 3:Example. Save
  8. Click Cards

    1. Choose Card Type 1

      • Front Template

        {{Name}} is a placeholder for the content written in the Name field.

        Wrapping it by {{#Name}} … {{/Name}} ensures that the card with the Name of the stylistic device on the front is only created if Name is non-empty.

        {{#Name}}
   {{Name}}
{{/Name}}

      • Back Template

        {{Name}}<br><br>
{{Definition}}<br><br>
{{Example}}

    2. Choose Card Type 2

      • Front Template 
        {{#Definition}}
   <br><br>
   {{Definition}}
{{/Definition}}
      • Back Template 
        {{Name}}<br><br>
{{Definition}}<br><br>
{{Example}}

    3. Click on Options (upper right corner) and Add Card Type

    4. Choose Card Type 3

      • Front Template 
        {{#Example}}
   <br><br><br><br>
   {{Example}}
{{/Example}}
      • Back Template 
        {{Name}}<br><br>
{{Definition}}<br><br>
{{Example}}
  9. Save all

2. Create a new Card using the Template

  1. Choose Cross Learning (Name, Definition, Example) as your Card Type

  2. Add context

  3. Save

  4. Repeat for more Cards

3. Learn

When you are done with creating cards you can start to learn them. You will be asked every card three times, with only the Name or the Definition or the Example given. (This sentence is a Polysyndeton by the way). You can also leave fields empty, then Anki won’t ask you those fields.

Have fun learning stylistic devices or any other content with the same structure.

This is my personal Java Summary. There’s nothing special about it, I just published it, because I already have it in markdown format, so why not?

A huge Thank You to https://www.w3schools.com/java/java_scope.asp. Most examples are more or less directly from the public Java Tutorial. Some of the more interesting I copied into my summary.

1. Basics

Compile & Run

C:\Users\Yourname\Path>javac Main.java	// Compile
C:\Users\Yourname\Path>java Main		// Execute

IO

int number = 5;
System.out.println("bla"+number);

Type casting

int x = 5;
double z = x; // Widening cast: z = 5.0, done automatically
int y = (int) z; // Narrowing cast: x = 5, need to specify the cast manually

Strings

String firstname = "Peter ";
String lastname = "Pan";
firstname.toUpperCase(); //PETER
firstname.toLowerCase(); //peter
firstname.length(); // 5
String name = firstname + lastname; // Peter Pan, or
String name = firstname.concat(lastname); // Peter Pan

String <-> Integer Conversion

String mystring = String.valueOf(myint); // if int myint = 5; -> mystring = "5"
int myint = Integer.valueOf(mystring); // if mystring = "10"; -> myint = 10;

Math helpers

Math.max(myint); Math.max(5,10); //10
Math.min(myint);
Math.abs(myint);
Math.sqrt(myint);
int randomNum = (int)(Math.random() * 101);  // 0 to 100

2. Conditions & Loops

If, else, elseif

if, else, else if as in C

if (x>y){
  // do …
}
else if (x==y){
  // do …
}
else { // (x<y)
  // do …
}

The available logical conditions are

Symbol Meaning
== equal to
< less than
<= less than or equal to
> greater than
>= greater than or equal to
!= not equal to

Ternary operators

if (x > y) {
	System.out.prinln("x>y");
} else {
	System.out.println("x<=y");
}

Can be written as:

(x>y) ? System.out.println("x>y") : System.out.println("x<=y");

while(condition){
	// do …
}

do while loop

do {
	// do …
}
while (condition);

Switch

switch (condition) {
	switch x: 
		// do …
		break;
	switch y: 
		// do …
		// if here no break, then condition z will also be executed

		// do …

	// do …

    Animal myCat = new Cat();  // Create a Pig object
    // myAnimal.animalSound(); // Execute the abstract function is not possible
    myCat.animalSound(); // The cat says: miau
  }
}

Interfaces

Notes on Interfaces from w3schools.

  • Like abstract classes, interfaces cannot be used to create objects (in the example above, it is not possible to create an “Animal” object in the MyMainClass)
  • Interface methods do not have a body - the body is provided by the “implement” class
  • On implementation of an interface, you must override all of its methods
  • Interface methods are by default abstract and public
  • Interface attributes are by default public, static and final
  • An interface cannot contain a constructor (as it cannot be used to create objects)

Why And When To Use Interfaces?

  1. To achieve security - hide certain details and only show the important details of an object (interface).

  2. Java does not support “multiple inheritance” (a class can only inherit from one superclass). However, it can be achieved with interfaces, because the class can implement multiple interfaces. Note: To implement multiple interfaces, separate them with a comma (see example below).

interface FirstInterface {
  public void myMethod(); // interface method, no body
}

interface SecondInterface {
  public void myOtherMethod(); // interface method, no body
}

class DemoClass implements FirstInterface, SecondInterface {
  public void myMethod() {
    System.out.println("Some text…");
  }
  public void myOtherMethod() {
    System.out.println("Some other text…");
  }
}

class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    DemoClass myObj = new DemoClass();
    myObj.myMethod();
    myObj.myOtherMethod();
  }
}

Enums

An enum represents a group of constants (public, final, static variables). Used for known, fix values, such as month names, weekdays, colors, etc. Handy if combined with the switch statement.

public class Main {
  enum Level {
    LOW, 
    MEDIUM,
    HIGH
  }
  public static void main(String[] args){
    Level myVar = Level.MEDIUM;
    System.out.println(myVar); //MEDIUM

    for (Level myVar : Level.values()){
      System.out.print(myVar+", "); //LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, 
    }
  }
}

Scanner

import java.util.Scanner;

class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args){
    Scanner myScanner = new Scanner(System.in);
    String inputString = myObj.nextLine();
  }
}
Method Description
nextBoolean() Reads a boolean value from the user
nextByte() Reads a byte value from the user
nextDouble() Reads a double value from the user
nextFloat() Reads a float value from the user
nextInt() Reads a int value from the user
nextLine() Reads a String value from the user
nextLong() Reads a long value from the user
nextShort() Reads a short value from the user

Date & Time

public class Main {

    LocalDate myDateObj = LocalDate.now(); // Create a date object
    LocalTime myTimeObj = LocalTime.now();
    LoclaDateTime myDateTimeObj = LocalDateTime.now();
    System.out.println(myDateObj); // 2025-04-01
    System.out.println(myTimeObj); // 20:20:01.123456
    System.out.println(myDateTimeObj); // 2025-04-01T20:20.01.123456
    DateTimeFormatter myFormatObj = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd-MM-yy HH:mm:ss");
    String formattedDate = myDateObj.format(myFormatObj);

  }
}

5. Java Data Structures

ArrayList

ArrayList class is a resizable arry in the java.util package (normal arrays are not resizable), where you can add/remove elements on the go.

Use Collections in the java.util package to sort lists. Will sort by default in ascending order. Use option Collections.reverseOrder() for descending order.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections; // Used to sort the ArrayList (alphabetically, ascending, etc. )

public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args){
    ArrayList<String> animals = new ArrayList<String>(); // Create new ArrayList object storing Strings
    // Instead of <String> one can use <Boolean>, <Character>, <Double>, <Integer>, etc. 
    animals.add("Zebra");
    animals.add("Mephitidae");
    animals.add("Cat")
    System.out.println(animals); // [Zebra, Mephitidae, Cat]
    animals.add(2,"Elephant"); // Specify position, start with 0
    System.out.println(animals); // [Zebra, Mephitidae, Elephant, Cat]
    System.out.println(animals.get(2)); // Elephant
    animals.set(2,"Dog"); // Overwrite Elephant
    animals.size(); 
    for (int i = 0; i < animals.size(); i++){
      // do …
    }
    Collections.sort(animals);
    System.out.println(animals); // [Cat, Dog, Mephitidae, Zebra]
    Collections.sort(animals, Collections.reverseOrder()); // Reverse the order
    System.out.println(animals); // [Zebra, Mephitidae, Dog, Cat]
    animals.remove(1); // Delete Mephitidae
    animals.clear(); // Empty ArrayList
  }
}

List of all useful ArrayList commands

LinkedList

Built as a linked list (like in C: structs referenced by pointers), whereas an ArrayList is a real array and if the array’s size is not sufficient anymore, a new, bigger array is reserved and all content copied over. Frontend-functionality is mostly the same.

List of all usefull LinkedList commands

HashMap

Hash maps are key/value pairs of same or different type, e.g. HashMap<String, String>, HashMap<String, boolean>, Hashmap<int, double> etc.

import java.util.HashMap();
public class Main{
  public static void main(String[] args){
    HashMap<String, String> Capitals = new HashMap<String, String>();
    Capitals.put("Germany", "Berlin");
    Capitals.put("England", "London");
    Capitals.put("France", "Paris");
    Capitals.put("Austria", "Vienna");
    System.out.println(Capitals); // {Germany=Berlin, England=London, France=Paris}
    System.out.println(Capitals.get("England")); // London
    System.out.println(Capitals.remove("Austria")); 
    System.out.println(Capitals.size()); // 3
    for (String myCountry : Capitals.keySet()){
      System.out.println(myCountry); // Germany, England, France
      System.out.println(myCountry+" is in "+myCountry.get(myCountry));
    }
    for (String myCapital : Capitals.value()){
      System.out.println(myCapital); // Berlin, London, Paris
    }
  }
}

HashSet

Purpose: Like an array, where each element exists only once, even if added multiple times.

Iterator

Used to iterate through an array, arraylist, hashmap, etc.

import java.util.Iterator;

Iterator<String> myiterator = animals.Iterator();
System.out.println(myiterator.next()); // Print first item
System.out.pirtnln(myiterator.next()); // Print second item
while (myiterator.hasNext() == true){
  currentanimal = myiterator.next(); // [Dog, Gnu, Zebra, ...]
  if(currentanumal == "Gnu"){
    myiterator.remove()
  }
}
System.out.println(myiterator); // [Dog, Zebra, ...] but no Gnu

Using a for loop or for-each loop would not work, as we are removing items from the array in situ (thus change it’s length), while we try to loop through it.

Wrapper Classes

Wrapper classes provide a way to use primitive variables as objects. The first character of the type classifier is written Uppercase, e.g. Char, Int, Double, etc. Useful if you work with arrays, arraylists where you can only store objects.

// ArrayList<int> mylist = new Arraylist<int>(); // Error
ArrayList<Integer> mylist = new ArrayList<Integer>(); // Works

// Create a new wrapper object
Integer myint = 5;

  • To get the object wrapper’s value: intValue(), byteValue(), shortValue(), longValue(), floatValue(), doubleValue(), charValue(), booleanValue().

  • To convert it to a String: .toString().

  • To get the length of the string

    Integer myint = 1000;
System.out.println(myint.toString().length()); // 4, as "1000" has four characters

6. Advanced stuff

Java Exceptions

try

If the block of code fails to be executed then run some failback code.

public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    try { // Initial code tried to get executed
      int[] myNumbers = {1, 2, 3};
      System.out.println(myNumbers[10]); // Out of bound error
    } catch (Exception e) { // error in try{} so execute this:
      System.out.println("Something went wrong.");
    } finally { // executed when try-catch is finished
      System.out.println("The 'try catch' is finished.");
    }
  }
}

throw

Use throw to throw a custom error of type ArithmeticException, FileNotFoundException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, SecurityException.

throw new ArithmeticException("Some error message");

item.title: How to include Scalable Vector Graphics (svg) in $\LaTeX$
item.description:
You may know the popular LaTeX package graphicx which you can use as:

\includegraphics[options]{filename}

graphicx does not support svg, but there is the package called svg that does the job.

How to use the svg package:

  1. Install Inkscape

    On Windows you can use winget.

    winget install -e --id Inkscape.Inkscape

  2. Copy your image.svg file into your document root folder (= right next to your .tex file)

  3. This is a MWE for your .tex file:

    \documentclass{article}
\includepackage{svg}
\begin{document}
    \begin{figure}
        \includesvg[]{image}
    \end{figure}
\end{document}

Notes:

  • File ending is optional (image or image.svg both work)
  • There are many parameters one can set in the square brackets (e.g. width=1cm, height=1cm, scale=0.5, and many more)
  • Download and read the svg package documentation on CTAN for more information

Oh no!

It would have been too easy. If you click on Build, you will run into an error:

example.tex: error: 120: Package svg Error: File `image_svg-tex.pdf' is missing. \includesvg{image}

You can solve this error by opening (in TeXstudio) Settings>Commands and adding the flag

--shell-escape

to your PdfLaTeX run command. The command now should look like:

pdflatex.exe -synctex=1 -interaction=nonstopmode --shell-escape %.tex

  • If you are using XeLaTeX, LulaTeX, etc. you should add the flag there (probably, I didn’t test it).

  • If you are using Texmaker, the whole idea is the same, but the exact settings may be somewhere else.

Save the configuration and run again.

More oh no!

We are not there yet. We need to solve the error message

example.tex: error: 119: Package svg Error: Inkscape version not detected. ...ncludesvg{image}

This error means that LaTeX doesn’t know where to find Inkscape. Therefore we add the path whereever inkscape was installed as a custom command. To do so, first locate the right folder (on Windows the default is: C:\Program Files\Inkscape\bin) then open Settings>Build and add the path to Commands.

That’s it, now it should run.
