item.title: Deploy Hugo on your Homeserver via GitHub Actions
item.description:
This is Part 2 of our Hugo publishing series. In Part 1: How to Create a Blog with Hugo and Smidr, we covered how to build and organize a modern blog locally using Hugo Extended and the Smidr theme.

Now, we take that setup to production on your own hardware. This guide covers how to deploy your Hugo website to a private Linux homeserver (such as a Raspberry Pi or home server) or VPS behind a Caddy web server.

Security Highlights of this Architecture

  • Port 22 (SSH) Remains Completely Closed: The home server pulls updates outbound over HTTPS or SSH Deploy Keys. No open inbound ports for SSH brute-force attackers.
  • Source Files Remain Private: Your Markdown drafts, unreleased posts, and configuration stay in your private GitHub repository (hugo-source).
  • Continuous Integration: GitHub Actions compiles the site with Hugo Extended and the Smidr theme submodule, then pushes only the static HTML/CSS to your deployment target.
  • Native SSL & Compression: Caddy handles automatic Let’s Encrypt certificates, HTTP/3, and Zstandard/Gzip compression out of the box.

Architectural Overview

[Local Workstation]
        │
        ▼ (git push: Markdown + Smidr Submodule)
[GitHub: hugo-source] (Private)
        │
        ▼ (GitHub Actions: Hugo Extended Build)
[GitHub: hugo-public] (Private Deploy Repo)
        ▲
        │ (Every 5 min: Outbound 'git pull' via SSH Deploy Key)
[Home Server / Raspberry Pi]
        ├── /var/www/hugo-public (Static Assets)
        └── Caddy Reverse Proxy (Ports 80/443 for Public Web Only)
  1. hugo-source (Private Repo): Houses your Markdown content, theme submodule (themes/smidr), and hugo.yaml.
  2. hugo-public (Private Repo): Stores only the compiled static HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images generated by Hugo.
  3. GitHub Actions: Whenever you push to hugo-source, the runner checks out submodules, builds the static site with hugo --minify, and pushes the result to hugo-public.
  4. Home Server: Runs a quiet cron job every 5 minutes that executes git pull using a read-only SSH Deploy Key. If changes are detected, Caddy serves them immediately.

Prerequisites

Before starting, ensure you have:

  1. A GitHub account.
  2. A private Hugo repository (hugo-source) set up with the Smidr theme (see Part 1).
  3. A Linux machine (Raspberry Pi, mini PC, or VPS) with Caddy installed.
  4. A domain name (or dynamic DNS like DuckDNS) pointing to your public home IP address.
  5. Inbound router ports 80 and 443 forwarded to your server for web traffic. (Port 22 for SSH should remain closed).

Step 1: Create the Deployment Repository and Token

Because GitHub Actions runners operate within an isolated environment, we must grant the action on hugo-source permission to push compiled code into hugo-public.

1.1 Create the Target Repository

  1. Log into GitHub and create a new repository called hugo-public.
  2. Set the repository visibility to Private (or Public if you want anyone to inspect the compiled HTML).
  3. Initialize it with a README.md so that the default main branch is created.

1.2 Generate a Fine-Grained Personal Access Token

  1. In your GitHub profile, navigate to Settings → Developer Settings → Personal Access Tokens → Fine-grained tokens.
  2. Click Generate new token and name it hugo-compiler-token.
  3. Under Repository access, select Only select repositories and pick your hugo-public repo.
  4. Under Permissions, expand Repository permissions, find Contents, and set it to Read and Write.
  5. Click Generate token and copy the generated secret key.

1.3 Add the Secret to Your Source Repository

  1. Navigate to your hugo-source repository on GitHub.
  2. Go to Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret.
  3. Set the name to PUBLIC_REPO_TOKEN and paste the token from the previous step.

Step 2: Configure the GitHub Actions Workflow

In your local hugo-source repository, create .github/workflows/compile.yml:

name: Compile Hugo and Deploy to Public Repo

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # Step 1: Checkout source code and submodules (crucial for Smidr theme)
      - name: Checkout Source & Themes
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          submodules: true
          fetch-depth: 0

      # Step 2: Install Hugo Extended
      - name: Setup Hugo Extended
        uses: peaceiris/actions-hugo@v3
        with:
          hugo-version: 'latest'
          extended: true

      # Step 3: Compile minified static files
      - name: Build Static Site
        # Note: If your site uses environment-specific config, use: hugo --minify --environment rpi
        run: hugo --minify

      # Step 4: Push compiled HTML to the target deployment repository
      - name: Push to Target Repo
        uses: cpina/github-action-push-to-another-repository@main
        env:
          API_TOKEN_GITHUB: ${{ secrets.PUBLIC_REPO_TOKEN }}
        with:
          source-directory: 'public'
          destination-github-username: 'YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME'
          destination-repository-name: 'hugo-public'
          user-email: 'your-email@example.com'
          target-branch: 'main'
💡
Hugo Environments

If you run different configurations for local development, GitHub Pages, and your homeserver (e.g. config/_default/ and config/rpi/), you can target specific environments directly in the build step:

run: hugo --minify --environment rpi

This allows you to change the baseURL, analytics, or parameters without modifying your core source files.

Commit and push this file to your hugo-source repository:

git add .github/workflows/compile.yml
git commit -m "Add automated Hugo compilation workflow"
git push origin main

Under the Actions tab on GitHub, you should see the pipeline run and complete in under 60 seconds.

Step 3: Set Up a Read-Only SSH Deploy Key on Your Server

Your server needs read-only access to pull down updates from hugo-public without storing your personal GitHub account password or full write tokens.

Log into your home server terminal via local network and follow these steps:

3.1 Generate an Ed25519 Keypair

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/id_github_blog -C "homeserver-blog-puller"

Press Enter twice to leave the passphrase empty so automated scripts can authenticate without human interaction.

3.2 Add the Public Key to GitHub

Display the public key and copy it:

cat ~/.ssh/id_github_blog.pub
  1. Go to your hugo-public repository on GitHub.
  2. Navigate to Settings → Deploy Keys → Add deploy key.
  3. Title it homeserver-caddy-puller, paste the key, and leave “Allow write access” unchecked.

3.3 Configure SSH Client on Your Server

Edit ~/.ssh/config (create it if it doesn’t exist):

nano ~/.ssh/config

Add the following block:

Host github-blog
    HostName github.com
    User git
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_github_blog
    IdentitiesOnly yes

Ensure secure permissions:

chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config ~/.ssh/id_github_blog
chmod 644 ~/.ssh/id_github_blog.pub

3.4 Clone the Repository to the Web Root

Create the directory where Caddy will serve the site:

sudo mkdir -p /var/www/hugo-public
sudo chown -R $USER:$USER /var/www/hugo-public

Clone the repository using the SSH alias:

git clone git@github-blog:YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/hugo-public.git /var/www/hugo-public

Verify that the compiled HTML files are present:

ls -la /var/www/hugo-public

Step 4: Automate Pulls with a Silent Cron Job

Because the server initiates the pull outward to GitHub, no inbound firewall ports (like port 22) need to be open.

Open your user’s crontab editor:

crontab -e

Add the following line at the bottom:

*/5 * * * * cd /var/www/hugo-public && git pull origin main >/dev/null 2>&1
  • */5 * * * *: Checks for updates every 5 minutes.
  • cd /var/www/hugo-public && git pull: Fetches any new commits from GitHub. If there are no new commits, Git exits immediately with minimal resource usage.
  • >/dev/null 2>&1: Suppresses terminal output and emails when there are no errors.

Save and exit. Your server will now automatically stay in sync with your GitHub deployment repository.

Step 5: Configure the Caddy Web Server

Caddy is an ultra-fast, modern web server that provisions and renews SSL certificates from Let’s Encrypt completely automatically.

Open your Caddyfile:

sudo nano /etc/caddy/Caddyfile

Add your site configuration block:

your-domain.com {
    # Path to compiled static files
    root * /var/www/hugo-public

    # Serve static files directly
    file_server

    # Modern compression for blazing speed
    encode zstd gzip

    # Custom 404 page handling
    handle_errors {
        rewrite * /{err.status_code}.html
        file_server
    }
}
💡
Permissions

Ensure Caddy’s process can read the files:

sudo chmod -R 755 /var/www/hugo-public

Reload Caddy

Apply the changes to Caddy:

  • If running as a systemd service: 
    sudo systemctl reload caddy
  • If running via Docker Compose: 
    docker compose exec caddy caddy reload

Testing the Complete Pipeline

Your end-to-end publishing pipeline is now operational:

  1. Edit locally: Write or revise an article in your local website folder.
  2. Commit & Push: 
    git add -A
git commit -m "Publish new post on robotics"
git push origin main
  3. Automated Build: GitHub Actions detects the push, builds the site using Hugo Extended and the Smidr theme, and updates hugo-public.
  4. Automated Server Pull: Within 5 minutes, your server pulls down the new files via cron.
  5. Instant Delivery: Visit your domain in any browser — your new content is live, encrypted with HTTPS, and served at top speed!

Whether you want to host your blog for free on GitHub Pages or deploy it automatically to a self-hosted server, this guide covers everything from initial setup to production publishing.

This is Part 1 of our Hugo series:

  • Part 1 (This Guide): Setup, configuration, Smidr theme, leaf bundles, interactive widgets, and publishing.
  • Part 2: Deploy Hugo on your Homeserver via GitHub Actions — zero-trust automated deployment behind Caddy without opening SSH ports.

Architecture: How Hugo and GitHub Work Together

A Hugo blog setup is clean and modular:

[Local Desktop]
   ├── Content (Markdown)
   ├── Configuration (hugo.yaml)
   └── Themes (Smidr via Git Submodule)
         │
         ├── (Local Preview: hugo server at localhost:1313)
         │
         ▼ (Git Push to Private Source Repo)
[GitHub: hugo-source]
         │
         ▼ (GitHub Actions Build: hugo --minify)
[Deployment Target]
   ├── Option A: GitHub Pages (https://<username>.github.io)
   └── Option B: Private Server / Raspberry Pi via Caddy
  1. Source Repository (website or hugo-source): Stores your Markdown drafts, images, configuration files, and theme submodules. This can be private to keep drafts and unpublished posts confidential.
  2. Compiled Static Output (public/): When Hugo runs, it compiles Markdown and layouts into blazing-fast, static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  3. Deployment Target: Served either directly by GitHub Pages (free, public repository <username>.github.io) or pulled down by your own Linux server using automated pipelines.

Prerequisites

Before beginning, install the required development tools for your platform.

1. Terminal

  • Windows: Use PowerShell 7+ rather than legacy Command Prompt (cmd.exe). You can install or update PowerShell via winget: 
    winget install -e --id Microsoft.PowerShell
  • Linux & macOS: Your default terminal (bash or zsh) works out of the box.

2. Git & GitHub

You need a GitHub account and Git installed locally:

  • Windows: 
    winget install -e --id Git.Git
    (Optional: Install GitHub Desktop via winget install -e --id GitHub.GitHubDesktop if you prefer a graphical authentication helper).
  • Linux (Debian/Ubuntu): 
    sudo apt update && sudo apt install git
  • macOS: 
    brew install git

Authenticate your Git installation using an SSH key or GitHub CLI (gh auth login).

Step 1: Install Hugo Extended

💡
Hugo Extended Required
The Extended edition of Hugo is strictly required for the Smidr theme because it uses Hugo’s advanced asset pipeline for Sass/SCSS compilation, CSS minification, and fingerprinting.
  • Windows: 
    winget install Hugo.Hugo.Extended
  • macOS (Homebrew): 
    brew install hugo
  • Linux: Download the latest extended .deb package or tarball from the Hugo GitHub Releases page: 
    hugo version
    Verify that the output displays +extended (e.g. hugo v0.125.0+extended ...).

Step 2: Initialize Your Source Repository

Create your central repository to store your Markdown articles, configuration, and assets.

  1. On GitHub, create a new private repository called website (or hugo-source).
  2. Open your terminal, navigate to your development directory, and clone the empty repository: 
    cd "C:/Projects" # or ~/Projects on Linux/macOS
git clone https://github.com/yourusername/website.git
cd website
  3. Initialize a new Hugo site inside the directory: 
    hugo new site . --force
    Note: Using . creates the Hugo directory structure directly inside your cloned git repository.

Step 3: Install the Smidr Theme

Smidr is a cyber-clean, dark-aesthetic Hugo theme designed for engineers, researchers, and developers. Key features include:

  • In-Browser Interactive Code Execution: Execute Python and JavaScript directly in the browser using WebAssembly (Pyodide).
  • Bilingual / Multilingual Ready: Side-by-side language switching (.en.md and .de.md).
  • LaTeX / KaTeX Mathematics: Blazing fast rendering for equations ( $$E=mc^2$$).
  • Dynamic Sidebar Filter & Search: Multi-checkbox taxonomy filters with AND/OR match modes, instant sorting, and Cmd+K / Ctrl+K modal search.
  • RSS Feeds with Beautiful XSLT Stylesheets: Clean, readable feeds for browsers and feed readers.

Install Smidr as a Git submodule so you can easily pull upstream updates:

git submodule add https://github.com/jokobus/smidr.git themes/smidr

To update the theme in the future:

git submodule update --remote --merge

Step 4: Configure Hugo and Smidr

Hugo supports both single-file configurations (hugo.yaml) and modular directory configurations (config/_default/). We recommend the modern, clean hugo.yaml format.

Create or update hugo.yaml in your project root (or inside config/_default/hugo.yaml):

baseURL: "https://yourusername.github.io/"
title: "My Tech Logbook"
theme: "smidr"
defaultContentLanguage: "en"
enableRobotsTXT: true

# Multi-output formats (required for Smidr fuzzy search & RSS)
outputs:
  home:
    - HTML
    - RSS
    - JSON # Powers client-side Ctrl+K search
  page:
    - HTML
  section:
    - HTML
    - RSS
  taxonomy:
    - HTML
  term:
    - HTML

# Taxonomies
taxonomies:
  category: "categories"
  tag: "tags"
  archive: "archives"

# Multilingual Configuration
languages:
  en:
    label: "English"
    locale: "en-US"
    weight: 1
    title: "My Tech Logbook"
    menus:
      main:
        - name: "Home"
          identifier: "home"
          url: "/"
          weight: 10
        - name: "Blog"
          identifier: "posts"
          url: "/posts/"
          weight: 20
        - name: "About"
          identifier: "about"
          url: "/about/"
          weight: 30
        - name: "Contact"
          identifier: "contact"
          url: "/contact/"
          weight: 40

  de:
    label: "Deutsch"
    locale: "de-DE"
    weight: 2
    title: "Mein Tech Logbuch"
    menus:
      main:
        - name: "Start"
          identifier: "home"
          url: "/"
          weight: 10
        - name: "Blog"
          identifier: "posts"
          url: "/posts/"
          weight: 20
        - name: "Über mich"
          identifier: "about"
          url: "/about/"
          weight: 30
        - name: "Kontakt"
          identifier: "contact"
          url: "/contact/"
          weight: 40

# Goldmark Markdown & KaTeX Math Parser
markup:
  goldmark:
    renderer:
      unsafe: true
    extensions:
      passthrough:
        enable: true
        delimiters:
          block:
            - ['\[', '\]']
            - ['$$', '$$']
          inline:
            - ['\(', '\)']
            - ['$', '$']
  highlight:
    noClasses: false
    style: "dracula"

Place these parameters in config/_default/params.yaml (or under params: in your hugo.yaml):

author:
  name: "Your Name"
  email: "hello@example.com"

subtitle: "Robotics, Machine Learning & Engineering"
description: "A fast, cyber-clean logbook powered by Hugo and Smidr."
since: 2024

# Features
math: true
showReadingTime: true

social:
  github: "yourusername"

social_media:
  items:
    - enabled: true
      title: "GitHub"
      link: "https://github.com/yourusername"

To ensure every new post automatically has the correct metadata, edit archetypes/default.md:

---
title: "{{ replace .File.ContentBaseName "-" " " | title }}"
description: ""
translationKey: "{{ replace .File.ContentBaseName "-" " " | title | lower }}"
author: "Your Name"
date: {{ .Date }}
archives: ["{{ dateFormat "2006-01" .Date }}"]
categories: ["Guide"]
tags: []
draft: true
toc: true
---

Step 5: Content Organization with Multilingual Leaf Bundles

The cleanest and most robust way to organize blog articles in Hugo is using Leaf Bundles. Instead of maintaining disjointed content/en/ and content/de/ trees, keep each post’s language files and assets together in a single folder:

content/
├── about.en.md
├── about.de.md
├── contact.en.md
├── contact.de.md
└── posts/
    └── my-first-post/
        ├── index.en.md       <-- English version
        ├── index.de.md       <-- German version
        └── images/           <-- Post-specific diagrams & assets
            └── architecture.svg

1. Create a New Post Bundle

Run the Hugo CLI to generate the bundle:

hugo new posts/my-first-post/index.en.md

2. Add Multilingual Support

To offer the article in German, duplicate index.en.md as index.de.md in the exact same directory:

cp content/posts/my-first-post/index.en.md content/posts/my-first-post/index.de.md

Open index.de.md, translate the content, and ensure both files share the exact same translationKey:

---
title: "Mein erster Beitrag"
translationKey: "my-first-post"
...
---

Hugo and Smidr will automatically link the two versions, enabling the instant language switcher in the header!

Step 6: Supercharge Posts with Smidr Shortcodes

Smidr includes built-in interactive components designed for technical articles:

1. In-Browser Python / WASM Code Runner

Allow readers to run and experiment with Python code right in their browser without installing anything:

{{< code-runner lang="python" title="Interactive Matrix Multiplication" >}}
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]])
C = np.dot(A, B)

print("Matrix Multiplication Result:")
print(C)
{{< /code-runner >}}

2. Cyber Callouts & Alerts

Highlight key insights or warnings using styled alert boxes:

{{< alert type="tip" title="Pro Tip" >}}
Run `hugo server -D` to preview draft posts locally before pushing to production.
{{< /alert >}}

Supported alert types: info, tip, warning, caution, robotics.

3. Mathematical Typesetting (KaTeX)

Write LaTeX math directly in your Markdown using $$:

$$
f(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}
$$

Step 7: Preview Locally

Start Hugo’s local development server to preview your site with instant live reloading:

hugo server -D

Open http://localhost:1313/ in your browser. Every time you save an edit in your editor, the page reloads automatically in milliseconds.

Step 8: Publishing Your Blog

There are two primary ways to publish your site:

Method A: Automated GitHub Actions CI/CD (Recommended)

Instead of compiling HTML manually on your machine, let GitHub Actions compile and publish your site automatically whenever you push Markdown.

  1. On GitHub, create a public repository named yourusername.github.io.
  2. Generate a Fine-Grained Personal Access Token with read/write permissions for yourusername.github.io.
  3. Add the token to your private website repository secrets as PUBLIC_REPO_TOKEN.
  4. Add the following workflow to .github/workflows/deploy.yml in your source repo:
name: Deploy Hugo Site

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout Source & Themes
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          submodules: true
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Setup Hugo Extended
        uses: peaceiris/actions-hugo@v3
        with:
          hugo-version: 'latest'
          extended: true

      - name: Build Minified Site
        run: hugo --minify

      - name: Push to GitHub Pages Repository
        uses: cpina/github-action-push-to-another-repository@main
        env:
          API_TOKEN_GITHUB: ${{ secrets.PUBLIC_REPO_TOKEN }}
        with:
          source-directory: 'public'
          destination-github-username: 'yourusername'
          destination-repository-name: 'yourusername.github.io'
          user-email: 'hello@example.com'
          target-branch: 'main'

Every git push to your source repository will now automatically compile and deploy your site in under 60 seconds!

Method B: Local Helper Script (Manual Publishing)

If you prefer building locally and pushing to GitHub Pages manually, use a helper script to automate the build and commit steps:

PowerShell Helper (gitcommit.ps1 for Windows):

$message = Read-Host "Enter Commit Message"
if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($message)) { $message = "Update blog content" }

Write-Host "--- 1. Pushing Source Repository ---" -ForegroundColor Cyan
git add -A
git commit -m $message
git push origin main

Write-Host "--- 2. Compiling Static Output ---" -ForegroundColor Cyan
hugo --minify

Write-Host "--- 3. Pushing Deployment Repository ---" -ForegroundColor Cyan
Set-Location -Path "public"
git add -A
git commit -m $message
git push origin main

Set-Location -Path ".."
Write-Host "Website successfully deployed!" -ForegroundColor Green

Step 9: Crawlers, SEO & RSS Feeds

1. Robots.txt

When enableRobotsTXT: true is enabled in hugo.yaml, Hugo generates robots.txt automatically. If you want to block search engine web crawlers completely from indexing your site, create layouts/robots.txt:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /

2. Custom RSS Feed with Smidr XSLT Styling

Smidr includes a custom XML stylesheet for RSS feeds (static/rss-style.xsl). Browsers that open /index.xml will render a dark-styled cyber feed rather than an unformatted XML tree, giving your readers a clean RSS subscription experience.

Next Steps: Self-Hosting on Your Own Server

Want to host your Hugo blog on your own Raspberry Pi, VPS, or home server behind a reverse proxy without opening SSH port 22?

Proceed to Part 2 of this guide: 👉 Deploy Hugo on your Homeserver via GitHub Actions

item.description:
Overview

Why and when do we need linear regression? In a nutshell, linear regression is used to predict data that has a linear relationship. That means all the datapoints are roughly on a straight line (in 2D), resp. on a hyperplane (in 3D). Firstly, we find some expression for the linear relationship (e.g. in 2D: $y=a\cdot x + b$; where $a$ is the slope and $b$ is the y-intercept). Secondly, we use this expression to insert some data where we only know the $x$ value, but want to predict their unknown $y$ value.

Linear regression with one variable

To get a feeling and understanding what linear regression is, we start with the most simple version: The 2D linear regression with one variable.

Figure 1 shows some datapoints, which are roughly linearly lined up. The expression for the blue regression line is: $y=a\cdot x + b$; where $a$ is the slope and $b$ is the y-intercept.

Find best regression line

First, we find $a$ and $b$ such that some error is minimized. Most datapoints are not on exactly on the regression line. Thus the $x$-$y$-relationship of each datapoint $i$ is not simply $y_i=a\cdot x_i + b$, but actually $y_i=a\cdot x_i + b + \varepsilon _i$ where $\varepsilon _i$ is the error we want to minimize. We can rewrite the expression and get $\varepsilon_i = y_i - (ax_i+b)$ where $y_i$ is the actual value and $- (ax_i+b)$ is the predicted value.

Now, what do we actually want to achieve? We want to minimize the total error $\varepsilon$ which is some ‘compound’ of all $\varepsilon_i$.

To get $\varepsilon$ we could try one of the following:

  • add up all $\varepsilon_i$ -> not a good idea as positive and negative $\varepsilon_i$ cancel each other
  • add up the absolute value of all $\varepsilon_i$ -> not that smart, because $\varepsilon$ won’t be differentiable anymore
  • add up the squares: $\varepsilon_i^2$ -> That is the so called least squared method (aka Euclidean Norm). Perfect!

Next, we compute the least squares. We want to minimize some function $f(a,b)$.

$f(a,b) = \sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-ax_i-b)^2$, where $n$ is the number of $x$-$y$-pairs we have

We take the derivatives wrt. to $a$ and $b$ and set them equal to zero.

I) $f_a = \frac{\partial f(a,b)}{\partial a} = \sum_{i=1}^n -2 (y_i-ax_i-b) x_i = 0$

II) $f_b = \frac{\partial f(a,b)}{\partial b} = \sum_{i=1}^n -2 (y_i-ax_i-b) = 0$

Then we do the math: (Note that we simply ommit the -2 first)

I) $0 =\sum y_i x_i - \sum a x_i^2 - \sum b x_i = \sum y_i x_i - a \sum x_i^2 - b\sum x_i $

II) $0 =\sum y_i - \sum a x_i - \sum b = \sum y_i - a \sum x_i - nb $

from II) $nb = \sum y_i - a \sum x_i$

II) in I) $0 =\sum y_i x_i - \sum a x_i^2 - (\frac{\sum y_i}{n} - \frac{a\sum x_i}{n})$

$\sum y_i x_i - \frac{\sum x_i\cdot \sum y_i}{n} = a (\sum x_i^2 - \frac{\sum x_i \cdot \sum x_i}{n})$

$ a = \frac{\sum x_i \sum y_i - n \sum x_iy_i}{(\sum x_i)^2 - n \sum x_i^2}$

$ b = \frac{\sum y_i - a \sum x_i}{n}$

That’s it. Now we have two expressions how we can find $a$ and $b$ of a given dataset.

Everything we need to do is to plug in all the data into the formulas for $a$ and $b$. Then we can take some unknow datapoint where we only have $x_i$, but not the corresponding $y_i$. We insert $x_i$ into our formula of $y_i = ax_i+b$ and we will get the $y_i$ value.

In case we leave 2D and want to solve problems in higher dimensions, we could do exactly the same procedure. In 3D we have $y_i = ax + bz + c$ and can solve the three resulting equalities to find some formulas for $a$, $b$ and $c$. However, the more dimensions we get, the more computation expensive this will become. Luckily, there is a smarter way, the Normal Equation of Linear Regression. We will come to that later.

Example

Consider the following five datapoints: (0,1), (1,1), (2,2), (3,2), (4,3)

$ a = \frac{\sum x_i \sum y_i - n \sum x_iy_i}{(\sum x_i)^2 - n \sum x_i^2} = \frac{5\cdot(0\cdot 1 + 1\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 2 + 3\cdot 2 + 4\cdot 3)- (0+1+2+3+4)\cdot (1+1+2+2+3)}{5\cdot(0^2+1^2+2^2+3^2+4^2)-(0+1+2+3+4)^2} = \frac{115-90}{150-100} = \frac{25}{50} = 0.5$

$ b = \frac{\sum y_i - a \sum x_i}{n} = \frac{1+1+2+2+3-0.5\cdot(0+1+2+3+4)}{5} = \frac{9-5}{5} = 0.8$

Thus, the final equation is $y = 0.5x+0.8$

If we want to predict the y-value for $x=2$, we get: $y=0.5\cdot2+0.8 = 1.8 \not = 2$. That is correct and makes sense, as our regression line does not perfectly go through each point, but rather minimizes the overall error.

Assumptions

The previous example worked very well. However, our data needs to fulfill specific requirements.

  1. Linearity: A linear relationship between all $x$ and $y$ datapoints
  2. Homoscedasticity: The variance of error is independent of $x$
  3. Normality: The data is normally distributed
  4. Independence: Each measurements/datapoint is independent from other measurements/datapoints

If those four requirements are fulfilled, we can use linear regression.

Linearization of non-linear models

Some real-life data may be not linear. E.g. the growth of bacteria-population is exponentially distributed. There are some tricks, how we can linearize some non-linear data, s.t. linear regression is applicable.

The following table shows some of the more common models and their linearization.

Name of Model Formula of Model Linearized Model Explanation/Hint
Exponnential distribution $y=a\cdot exp(bx)$ $ln(y) = bx + ln(a)$ Take natural logarithm on both sides of the equation.
Power Model $y=ax^b$ $ln(y) = ln(a) + bln(x)$ Take natural logaritm.
Saturation Model $y = \frac{ax}{b-x}$ $\frac{1}{y} = \frac{1}{x} \frac{b}{a} + \frac{1}{a}$ Reverse fractions, then simplify
Polynomial Regression $y = a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+a_{n-2}x^{n-2}+...+a_1x^1+a_0$ Not so simple, see below.

The polynomial Regression needs a little bit more text.

Polynomial Regression of order m=2 (quadratic)

We have $y = a_2x^2+a_1x^1+a_0 + \varepsilon$ and the next steps are actually pretty close to what we did above to find the best regression line.

The sum of the squares of the errors $S = \sum_i \big((y_i-a-bx_i-cx_i^2)^2\big)$. Differentiating wrt. $a$, $b$ and $c$ we get:

I) $an + bS_1+cS_2 = S_5$

II) $aS_1 + bS_2+cS_3 = S_6$

III) $aS_2 + bS_3+cS_4 = S_7$

where $S_1 = \sum_i x_i$

$S_2 = \sum_i x_i^2$

$S_3 = \sum_i x_i^3$

$S_4 = \sum_i x_i^4$

$S_5 = \sum_i y_i$

$S_6 = \sum_i x_iy_i$

$S_7 = \sum_i x_i^2y_i$

Do you see the pattern?

Polynomial regression for any order m

If yes, then the following might be interesting to you. It is (with a small modification) taken from the Wikipedia-Article about Polynomial Regression. Solving this linear system for the $a_i$’s will work for any polynomial power $m$.

$ \left[ \begin{matrix} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^0 & \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^1 & \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 & \cdots & \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^m \\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^1 & \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 & \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^3 & \cdots & \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^{m+1} \\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 & \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^3 & \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^4 & \cdots & \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^{m+2} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^m & \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^{m+1} & \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^{m+2} & \cdots & \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^{2m} \\ \end{matrix} \right] $ $ \left[ \begin{matrix} a_0 \\ a_1 \\ a_2 \\ \vdots \\ a_m \\ \end{matrix} \right] $ $=\left[ \begin{matrix} \sum_{i=0}^n y_i x_i^0 \\ \sum_{i=0}^n y_i x_i^1 \\ \sum_{i=0}^n y_i x_i^2 \\ \vdots \\ \sum_{i=0}^n y_i x_i^m \\ \end{matrix} \right] $

Normal Equation of Linear Regression

So far we mainly talked about linear regression in 2D and realized that doing linear regression in higher dimensions is analog to 2D, but very includes a lot of work. Luckily, as already mentioned, there is an easier way to do linear regression for higher dimensions.

Normal Equation of Linear Regression in 2D

Derivation

$\vec u=\vec b-x\vec a$

min $\frac12 (\vec b - x\vec a)^2$

$\frac{d}{d\vec a} \frac12 (\vec b - x\vec a)^2 = (\vec b - x\vec a)\vec a = 0$

$ \vec b\cdot\vec a - x\vec a\cdot\vec a = 0$

$x = \frac{\vec b\cdot\vec a}{\vec a\cdot\vec a}$

To get the general solution for the least squares method in n-dimensions we do the following steps:

$\varepsilon(x) = (\vec a x - \vec b)^2 = (\vec a x - \vec b)^T (\vec a x - \vec b) = (\vec a x)^T (\vec a x) - (\vec a x)^T \vec b - \vec a x \vec b^T + \vec b^T\vec b = x^2\vec a^T\vec a - x(\vec a^T\vec b+\vec b^T\vec a)+\vec b^T\vec b = x^2\vec a^T\vec a - 2x\vec a^T\vec b+\vec b^T\vec b$

$\frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial x} = 2x\vec a^T\vec a -2\vec a^T\vec b = 0$

$x\vec a^T\vec a -\vec a^T\vec b = 0$

Th gives the general solution for the least squares method in n-dimensions:

$$x=\frac{\vec a^T\vec b}{\vec a^T\vec a}$$

Example

Let $\vec a = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\\end{pmatrix}$ and $\vec b = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \\\end{pmatrix}$ then $\varepsilon (x) = (2x-1)^2+(3x-2)^2+(4x-3)^2 \rightarrow \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial x} = 2(2x-1)+2(3x-2)+2(4x-3) = 0 \Leftrightarrow (2x-1)+(3x-2)+(4x-3) = 0$. This equation can be solved for $x$ and you will get $x=\frac23$.

Normal Equation in Multiple Dimensions

In the general multivariate case with $m$ features and $n$ training observations:

Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (m+1)}$ denote the design matrix with a leading column of ones representing the intercept $b$, and let $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be the target vector. Our goal is to find the optimal parameter vector $\theta = [b, a_1, \dots, a_m]^T$ that minimizes the residual sum of squares:

$$J(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \|X\theta - y\|^2 = \frac{1}{2} (X\theta - y)^T (X\theta - y)$$

Expanding the quadratic matrix form:

$$J(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \left( \theta^T X^T X \theta - 2 y^T X \theta + y^T y \right)$$

Taking the gradient with respect to $\theta$ and setting it to zero:

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = X^T X \theta - X^T y = 0$$$$X^T X \theta = X^T y$$

Assuming $X^T X$ is invertible (non-singular), we obtain the analytical Normal Equation:

$$\mathbf{\theta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y}$$
💡
Tip
Closed-Form vs. Gradient Descent: The Normal Equation yields the globally optimal weights in a single step without choosing a learning rate $\alpha$ or iterating. However, computing the matrix inverse $(X^T X)^{-1}$ scales as $\mathcal{O}(m^3)$, making iterative Gradient Descent preferable when the feature count $m > 10^4$.

$\vec u=\vec b-x\vec a$

min $\frac12 (\vec b - x\vec a)^2$

$\frac{d}{d\vec a} \frac12 (\vec b - x\vec a)^2 = (\vec b - x\vec a)\vec a = 0$

$ \vec b\cdot\vec a - x\vec a\cdot\vec a = 0$

$x = \frac{\vec b\cdot\vec a}{\vec a\cdot\vec a}$

To get the general solution for the least squares method in n-dimensions we do the following steps:

$\varepsilon(x) = (\vec a x - \vec b)^2 = (\vec a x - \vec b)^T (\vec a x - \vec b) = (\vec a x)^T (\vec a x) - (\vec a x)^T \vec b - \vec a x \vec b^T + \vec b^T\vec b = x^2\vec a^T\vec a - x(\vec a^T\vec b+\vec b^T\vec a)+\vec b^T\vec b = x^2\vec a^T\vec a - 2x\vec a^T\vec b+\vec b^T\vec b$

$\frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial x} = 2x\vec a^T\vec a -2\vec a^T\vec b = 0$

$x\vec a^T\vec a -\vec a^T\vec b = 0$

Th gives the general solution for the least squares method in n-dimensions:

$$x=\frac{\vec a^T\vec b}{\vec a^T\vec a}$$

Example

Let $\vec a = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\\end{pmatrix}$ and $\vec b = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \\\end{pmatrix}$ then $\varepsilon (x) = (2x-1)^2+(3x-2)^2+(4x-3)^2 \rightarrow \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial x} = 2(2x-1)+2(3x-2)+2(4x-3) = 0 \Leftrightarrow (2x-1)+(3x-2)+(4x-3) = 0$. This equation can be solved for $x$ and you will get $x=\frac23$.

Normal Equation in Multiple Dimensions

In the general multivariate case with $m$ features and $n$ training observations:

Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (m+1)}$ denote the design matrix with a leading column of ones representing the intercept $b$, and let $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be the target vector. Our goal is to find the optimal parameter vector $\theta = [b, a_1, \dots, a_m]^T$ that minimizes the residual sum of squares:

$$J(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \|X\theta - y\|^2 = \frac{1}{2} (X\theta - y)^T (X\theta - y)$$

Expanding the quadratic matrix form:

$$J(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \left( \theta^T X^T X \theta - 2 y^T X \theta + y^T y \right)$$

Taking the gradient with respect to $\theta$ and setting it to zero:

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = X^T X \theta - X^T y = 0$$$$X^T X \theta = X^T y$$

Assuming $X^T X$ is invertible (non-singular), we obtain the analytical Normal Equation:

$$\mathbf{\theta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y}$$
💡
Tip
Closed-Form vs. Gradient Descent: The Normal Equation yields the globally optimal weights in a single step without choosing a learning rate $\alpha$ or iterating. However, computing the matrix inverse $(X^T X)^{-1}$ scales as $\mathcal{O}(m^3)$, making iterative Gradient Descent preferable when the feature count $m > 10^4$.

item.title: Backpropagation in Matrix Calculus
item.description:
Introduction

In our previous article, Backpropagation in Standard Calculus, we derived the gradient update equations using scalar notation. While standard calculus builds an intuitive understanding of how error flows through individual connections, writing code using scalar loops is computationally inefficient.

In practice, modern machine learning libraries (like PyTorch or TensorFlow) compute updates over entire layers simultaneously using Matrix Calculus and linear algebra routines optimized for GPUs.

This article formalizes backpropagation in vector and matrix notation.

Mathematical Conventions & Notation

We treat all vectors as column vectors unless transposed.

For a network with $L$ layers:

  • $l \in \{1, 2, \dots, L\}$ denotes the layer index ($l=0$ is the input layer).
  • $n_l$ is the number of neurons in layer $l$.
  • $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a}^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_0 \times 1}$ is the input vector.
  • $\mathbf{W}^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l \times n_{l-1}}$ is the weight matrix for layer $l$, where entry $W_{ij}^{(l)}$ connects unit $j$ in layer $l-1$ to unit $i$ in layer $l$.
  • $\mathbf{b}^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l \times 1}$ is the bias vector for layer $l$.
  • $\mathbf{z}^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l \times 1}$ is the pre-activation linear combination.
  • $\mathbf{a}^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l \times 1}$ is the post-activation vector.

Side Note: The Hadamard Product ($\odot$)

When working with matrix calculus in neural networks, we frequently encounter element-wise operations. The Hadamard Product (also called the entrywise or element-wise product), denoted by $\odot$, multiplies corresponding elements of two matrices or vectors of identical dimensions.

Given two vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}$:

$$\mathbf{u} \odot \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \\ \vdots \\ u_n \end{bmatrix} \odot \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ \vdots \\ v_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 v_1 \\ u_2 v_2 \\ \vdots \\ u_n v_n \end{bmatrix}$$

Unlike standard matrix multiplication ($\mathbf{A} \mathbf{B}$), which sums dot products across rows and columns, the Hadamard product keeps the dimensions unchanged ($n \times 1$). We use it when applying nonlinear element-wise derivative functions $\sigma'(\mathbf{z})$ to error vectors.

Vectorized Forward Pass

For any layer $l \in \{1, \dots, L\}$, the forward pass calculations are expressed as:

$$\mathbf{z}^{(l)} = \mathbf{W}^{(l)} \mathbf{a}^{(l-1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(l)}$$$$\mathbf{a}^{(l)} = \sigma(\mathbf{z}^{(l)})$$

where $\sigma(\cdot)$ represents an element-wise activation function (e.g., Sigmoid, ReLU).

Loss Function

Using the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss over target vector $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_L \times 1}$ and network output $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{a}^{(L)}$:

$$E = \frac{1}{2} \Vert{}\mathbf{a}^{(L)} - \mathbf{t}\Vert{}^2 = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n_L} \left(a_i^{(L)} - t_i\right)^2$$

Vectorized Backpropagation

To update parameters via gradient descent, we need two target derivatives for each layer $l$:

  1. $\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(l)}}$ (a matrix of shape $n_l \times n_{l-1}$)
  2. $\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{b}^{(l)}}$ (a vector of shape $n_l \times 1$)

1. The Error Vector ($\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)}$)

We define the layer error vector $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)}$ as the gradient of the loss with respect to the unactivated weighted input $\mathbf{z}^{(l)}$:

$$\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)} \equiv \frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(l)}} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial E}{\partial z_1^{(l)}} \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\partial E}{\partial z_{n_l}^{(l)}} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_l \times 1}$$

2. Output Layer Error ($\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(L)}$)

Applying the multivariable chain rule to the final layer $L$:

$$\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(L)} = \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{a}^{(L)}}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(L)}} \right)^T \frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{a}^{(L)}}$$

Since $\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{a}^{(L)}} = (\mathbf{a}^{(L)} - \mathbf{t})$ and the Jacobian $\frac{\partial \mathbf{a}^{(L)}}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(L)}}$ is a diagonal matrix of activation derivatives $\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(L)}))$, this simplifies directly via the Hadamard product:

$$\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(L)} = (\mathbf{a}^{(L)} - \mathbf{t}) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(L)})$$

3. Layer Recurrence Relation ($\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)}$ from $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l+1)}$)

To propagate the error backwards from layer $l+1$ to layer $l$, we apply the chain rule:

$$\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(l)}} = \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(l+1)}}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(l)}} \right)^T \frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(l+1)}}$$

Given that $\mathbf{z}^{(l+1)} = \mathbf{W}^{(l+1)} \mathbf{a}^{(l)} + \mathbf{b}^{(l+1)}$ and $\mathbf{a}^{(l)} = \sigma(\mathbf{z}^{(l)})$, taking the Jacobian matrix $\frac{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(l+1)}}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(l)}}$ yields $\mathbf{W}^{(l+1)} \operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(l)}))$. Transposing and multiplying gives:

$$\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)} = \left( (\mathbf{W}^{(l+1)})^T \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l+1)} \right) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(l)})$$

This recursive relation allows computing all errors $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)}$ starting from $L$ down to $1$.

4. Parameter Gradients

With $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)}$ computed, parameter derivatives are evaluated as:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(l)}} = \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)} (\mathbf{a}^{(l-1)})^T$$$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{b}^{(l)}} = \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)}$$

Detailed Example: Unrolling Gradients to Layer 1

Consider a 3-layer neural network ($L=3$) with input vector $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a}^{(0)}$.

[ Input: x ] ---> [ Layer 1: W(1) ] ---> [ Layer 2: W(2) ] ---> [ Layer 3: W(3) ] ---> [ Output: y = a(3) ]

We want to find the exact unrolled gradient expression for the first weight matrix $\mathbf{W}^{(1)}$ in terms of the initial input $\mathbf{x}$, weights, activation derivatives, and error target $\mathbf{t}$.

Step 1: Compute Output Error $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(3)}$

$$\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(3)} = (\mathbf{a}^{(3)} - \mathbf{t}) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(3)})$$

Step 2: Propagate to Layer 2 Error $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(2)}$

Substitute $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(3)}$ into the recurrence formula:

$$\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(2)} = \left( (\mathbf{W}^{(3)})^T \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(3)} \right) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(2)})$$$$\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(2)} = \left( (\mathbf{W}^{(3)})^T \left[ (\mathbf{a}^{(3)} - \mathbf{t}) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(3)}) \right] \right) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(2)})$$

Step 3: Propagate to Layer 1 Error $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(1)}$

Substitute $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(2)}$ into the recurrence formula:

$$\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(1)} = \left( (\mathbf{W}^{(2)})^T \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(2)} \right) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(1)})$$

Substituting the full expression for $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(2)}$ yields:

$$\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(1)} = \left( (\mathbf{W}^{(2)})^T \left[ \left( (\mathbf{W}^{(3)})^T \left[ (\mathbf{a}^{(3)} - \mathbf{t}) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(3)}) \right] \right) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(2)}) \right] \right) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(1)})$$

Step 4: Final Unrolled Gradient for $\mathbf{W}^{(1)}$

Using $\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(1)}} = \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(1)} (\mathbf{a}^{(0)})^T$ where $\mathbf{a}^{(0)} = \mathbf{x}$:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(1)}} = \left( \left( (\mathbf{W}^{(2)})^T \left( (\mathbf{W}^{(3)})^T \left[ (\mathbf{a}^{(3)} - \mathbf{t}) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(3)}) \right] \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(2)}) \right) \right) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(1)}) \right) \mathbf{x}^T$$

Summary Matrix Reference Table

Quantity Formula Dimensions
Output Error $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(L)} = (\mathbf{a}^{(L)} - \mathbf{t}) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(L)})$ $n_L \times 1$
Backpropagated Error $\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)} = \left( (\mathbf{W}^{(l+1)})^T \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l+1)} \right) \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(l)})$ $n_l \times 1$
Weight Gradient $\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(l)}} = \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)} (\mathbf{a}^{(l-1)})^T$ $n_l \times n_{l-1}$
Bias Gradient $\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{b}^{(l)}} = \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)}$ $n_l \times 1$

item.title: Feedforward Phase
item.description:
Introduction

This article gives a quick overview over the feedforward phase of a Neural Network.

Nodes

A Neural Network is made of many Nodes that are connected to each other. Each Node itself is a very basic unit that does only do three things.

  1. Multiply each input with a weight and sum all inputs up. $y_{in} = \sum_{i=0}^m w_i\cdot x_i$, where $m$ is the number of inputs.
  2. Process the single, scalar input value by some activation function $y_{out}=f(y_{in})$ where $y_{in}$ is the result from step 1 and $y_{out}$ is the result from step 1 after being applied to the activation function.
  3. Output the result $y_{out}$ to the next node

So, a single node pretty much looks like this:

Here:

  1. $y_{in} = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + w_0x_0$ (where each x_i and w_i is a scalar of course)
  2. $y_{out} = f(y_{in})$

Bias

One special input we have to talk about is the bias $x_0$. Per definition $x_0 = 1$ always. The bias is needed as an offset. You can think of it as the multi-dimensional equivalent to the y-intercept in 2D. Without a y-intercept each function in 2D has to go through the center of the coordinate system. The same applies for our Node: With this offset, the Neural Network can e.g. classify data even if their optimal separation hyperplane does not go through the origin.

Example

Let’s say we have the following Node and the activation function $f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x > 0\\ 0 & \text{else } \end{cases}$

  1. $y_{in} = \sum_{i=0}^m w_i\cdot x_i = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + w_0x_0 = 1\cdot 2 + 2\cdot 4 + 3 \cdot 1 = 2+8+3 = 13$
  2. $y_{out} = f(y_{in})$. We have $y_{in} = 13 > 0$ so $y_{out} = 1$
  3. The node outputs $y_{out} = 1$
🧠 Interactive Single Neuron Visualizer
Input 1 ($x_1$): 2.0
Weight 1 ($w_1$): 1.0
Input 2 ($x_2$): 4.0
Weight 2 ($w_2$): 2.0
Bias ($w_0$ or $b$): 3.0
Net Input ($y_{in}$): 13.00
Neuron Output ($y_{out}$): 1.00

Activation functions

In the previous example we used the so called binary step function as our activation function. However, there are a few more I would like to mention here.

Function Formula Description
Identify function $f(x)=x$ Very basic
Binary step function $f(x) = \begin{cases}1 & \text{if } x > 0\\0 & \text{else }\end{cases}$
Bipolar step function $f(x) = \begin{cases}1 & \text{if } x > 0\\-1 & \text{else }\end{cases}$
Binary Sigmoid $f(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} = \frac{e^x}{e^x+e^{-x}}$
Bipolar Sigmiod $f(x) = \frac{2}{1+e^{-x}}+1 = \frac{e^x-e^{-x}}{e^x+e^{-x}} = tanh(x)$
ReLu (Rectified Linear Unit ) $f(x) = max(x,0)$
Softplus $f(x) = ln(1+e^x)$
Leaky ReLu $f(x)=\begin{cases}x & \text{if } x > 0\\\alpha x, \;\alpha\text{ small} & \text{else }\end{cases}$
Softmax $f(x_i)=\frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}}$

Architecture

Now we have seen how each node works. He gets some information, processes this information and outputs the result. That is not very impressing so far, but many of those nodes are combined in a specific Architecture, then they can perform powerful tasks.

Feedforward

The following plot shows a very basic Neural Network, that has 3 layers. One input layer $x$, one hidden layer $z$ and one output layer $y$. Between each consecutive layer we have connections $w$ and $v$. For the moment, we don’t care about how the weights were computed, as this is done by the training process. The feedforward part is used for predicting, the output for a given input. If we are testing the Neural Network, we use the feedforward method, as shown in this article. In the training part, we also use feedforward, but that is a topic for another article: Backpropgation

Each connection $w_{ij}$ is the weight from node $x_i$ to $z_j$. So, for example $w_{01}$ is the weight from $x_0$ (the bias!) to $z_1$.

Steps of Feedforward

  • For each layer (starting at the first hidden layer)
    • For each node in the layer
      1. $z_{in} = \sum_{i=0}^m w_i\cdot x_i$, where $m$ is the number of inputs. Resp. $y_{in} = \sum_{i=0}^p v_i\cdot z_i$, where $p$ is the number of inputs.
      2. Apply the activation function $z_{out}=f(z_{in})$, resp. $y_{out}=f(y_{in})$
      3. Output the result $z_{out}$ to the next layer, resp. $y_{out}$ to the output
    • End
  • End

Example

Let’s consider the following Neural Network. Each node has the binary step function $f(x) = \begin{cases}1 & \text{if } x > 0\\0 & \text{else }\end{cases}$ applied to it.

  • We begin with the hidden layer
    1. First we calculate all $z_{in}$ (Note that $x_0$ and $z_0$ are the biases, so $x_0=1$ and $z_0=1$ always. )
      • $z_{1,in} = w_{01}x_0+w_{11}x_1+w_{21}x_2 = 1\cdot 1+2\cdot 2+(-0.5)\cdot 3 = 3.5$

Introduction

This article gives a quick overview over the feedforward phase of a Neural Network.

Nodes

A Neural Network is made of many Nodes that are connected to each other. Each Node itself is a very basic unit that does only do three things.

  1. Multiply each input with a weight and sum all inputs up. $y_{in} = \sum_{i=0}^m w_i\cdot x_i$, where $m$ is the number of inputs.
  2. Process the single, scalar input value by some activation function $y_{out}=f(y_{in})$ where $y_{in}$ is the result from step 1 and $y_{out}$ is the result from step 1 after being applied to the activation function.
  3. Output the result $y_{out}$ to the next node

So, a single node pretty much looks like this:

Here:

  1. $y_{in} = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + w_0x_0$ (where each x_i and w_i is a scalar of course)
  2. $y_{out} = f(y_{in})$

Bias

One special input we have to talk about is the bias $x_0$. Per definition $x_0 = 1$ always. The bias is needed as an offset. You can think of it as the multi-dimensional equivalent to the y-intercept in 2D. Without a y-intercept each function in 2D has to go through the center of the coordinate system. The same applies for our Node: With this offset, the Neural Network can e.g. classify data even if their optimal separation hyperplane does not go through the origin.

Example

  2. $y_{out} = f(y_{in})$. We have $y_{in} = 13 > 0$ so $y_{out} = 1$
  3. The node outputs $y_{out} = 1$

Introduction

This article explains backpropagation of a Neural Network using standard scalar calculus notation. If you want to know how backpropagation is done using vectors and matrices, read this article: Backpropagation in Matrix Calculus

Learning Process

Consider a 2-layer Neural Network (one hidden layer and one output layer) as shown below. We want to train the network so that the training inputs $x$ correctly produce the expected target labels $t$.

For training, we use a dataset containing paired samples $(x, t)$. Each pair is used to adjust the network parameters to minimize the difference between the network’s prediction $y$ and the actual target $t$. Thinking of the network as a function $y = f(x)$, our goal is to adjust $f(x)$ until the prediction error is as small as possible. A smaller error means the predictions closely match ground truth labels.

Training this neural network comes down to finding weight values that yield predictions $y = f(x)$ as close as possible to the target $t$, especially on unseen test data.

Training Algorithm

The high-level training process follows this structure:

Loop over epochs
    Loop over all training samples (x, t)
        1. Feedforward pass (compute predictions y)
        2. Compute total error E between prediction y and target t
        3. Backpropagate error and calculate gradients
        4. Update weights using gradient descent
    End loop
End loop
  1. Feedforward phase: Covered in detail in the Article about the Feedforward Phase.
  2. Error calculation: Measured using the squared error sum:
$$E = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i (t_i - y_i)^2$$

For an output node $i$, the error contribution is $E_i = \frac{1}{2}(t_i - y_i)^2$. The factor $\frac{1}{2}$ is added so that taking derivative cancels the constant factor:

$$\frac{\partial E_i}{\partial y_i} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot (t_i - y_i) \cdot (-1) = -(t_i - y_i) = y_i - t_i$$
  1. Backpropagation phase: Applies the chain rule backwards through the network layers to calculate how much each weight contributed to the final error.

The Chain Rule

The goal of backpropagation is to calculate the derivative of the loss function $E$ with respect to every weight $w$ in the network: $\frac{\partial E}{\partial w}$. Once we know this rate of change, we can adjust the weight in the direction that decreases the error.

Since a weight deep in the network influences the output through a series of nested calculations, we use the calculus chain rule. For a composed function $y = f(g(x))$, the derivative with respect to $x$ is:

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{dg} \cdot \frac{dg}{dx}$$

In neural networks, we apply this rule step-by-step from the output layer backwards to the input layer.

1. Output Layer Weights

Let $w_{ij}^{(2)}$ be the weight connecting hidden unit $h_j$ to output unit $y_i$.

The output calculation at node $i$ consists of two steps:

  1. Weighted sum plus bias:
$$z_i^{(2)} = \sum_{j} w_{ij}^{(2)} h_j + b_i^{(2)}$$
  1. Activation function application (e.g., Sigmoid $\sigma$):
$$y_i = \sigma(z_i^{(2)})$$

To find how changes in $w_{ij}^{(2)}$ affect total loss $E$, we decompose $\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}}$ into three partial derivatives:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial y_i} \cdot \frac{\partial y_i}{\partial z_i^{(2)}} \cdot \frac{\partial z_i^{(2)}}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}}$$

Let’s compute each term:

  • Term 1: Derivative of error w.r.t. output prediction
$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial y_i} = (y_i - t_i)$$
  • Term 2: Derivative of activation function w.r.t. weighted sum
$$\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial z_i^{(2)}} = \sigma'(z_i^{(2)})$$

(For the sigmoid function $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, the derivative is $\sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))$).

  • Term 3: Derivative of weighted sum w.r.t. weight
$$\frac{\partial z_i^{(2)}}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}} = h_j$$

Combining these terms:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}} = (y_i - t_i) \cdot \sigma'(z_i^{(2)}) \cdot h_j$$

To simplify notation, define the error term (or local gradient) $\delta_i^{(2)}$ for output node $i$:

$$\delta_i^{(2)} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial z_i^{(2)}} = (y_i - t_i) \sigma'(z_i^{(2)})$$

This lets us express the gradient cleanly as:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}} = \delta_i^{(2)} h_j$$

2. Hidden Layer Weights

Now consider weight $w_{jk}^{(1)}$ in the first layer, connecting input $x_k$ to hidden node $h_j$.

The weighted sum and activation for hidden node $h_j$ are:

$$z_j^{(1)} = \sum_{k} w_{jk}^{(1)} x_k + b_j^{(1)}$$$$h_j = \sigma(z_j^{(1)})$$

Hidden node $h_j$ feeds into all output nodes in the next layer. Therefore, changing $w_{jk}^{(1)}$ alters $h_j$, which propagates through every output node $i$. By the multivariate chain rule, we sum the contributions over all output nodes $i$:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}^{(1)}} = \left( \sum_{i} \frac{\partial E}{\partial z_i^{(2)}} \cdot \frac{\partial z_i^{(2)}}{\partial h_j} \right) \cdot \frac{\partial h_j}{\partial z_j^{(1)}} \cdot \frac{\partial z_j^{(1)}}{\partial w_{jk}^{(1)}}$$

Breaking down these components:

  • From the output layer analysis, $\frac{\partial E}{\partial z_i^{(2)}} = \delta_i^{(2)}$.
  • The derivative of output linear combination w.r.t hidden activation is:
$$\frac{\partial z_i^{(2)}}{\partial h_j} = w_{ij}^{(2)}$$
  • The activation derivative is:
$$\frac{\partial h_j}{\partial z_j^{(1)}} = \sigma'(z_j^{(1)})$$
  • The derivative w.r.t the weight itself is:
$$\frac{\partial z_j^{(1)}}{\partial w_{jk}^{(1)}} = x_k$$

Substituting these back into our expression gives:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}^{(1)}} = \left( \sum_{i} \delta_i^{(2)} w_{ij}^{(2)} \right) \cdot \sigma'(z_j^{(1)}) \cdot x_k$$

Defining the hidden layer error term $\delta_j^{(1)}$:

$$\delta_j^{(1)} = \left( \sum_{i} \delta_i^{(2)} w_{ij}^{(2)} \right) \sigma'(z_j^{(1)})$$

The gradient simplifies to:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}^{(1)}} = \delta_j^{(1)} x_k$$

Notice the pattern: for any weight connecting node $A$ to node $B$, the gradient is equal to the error term $\delta$ at node $B$ multiplied by the activation input from node $A$.

Updating Weights with Gradient Descent

Once gradients are computed for all weights and biases, parameters are updated in the direction opposite to the gradient to minimize total loss $E$:

$$w_{ij}^{(2)} \leftarrow w_{ij}^{(2)} - \eta \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}}$$$$w_{jk}^{(1)} \leftarrow w_{jk}^{(1)} - \eta \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}^{(1)}}$$

Where $\eta > 0$ is the learning rate, controlling the step size of each update. Biases are updated identically using their respective $\delta$ terms:

$$b_i^{(2)} \leftarrow b_i^{(2)} - \eta \, \delta_i^{(2)}$$$$b_j^{(1)} \leftarrow b_j^{(1)} - \eta \, \delta_j^{(1)}$$

Summary

Backpropagation breaks down loss optimization into two steps:

  1. Forward Pass: Compute activation outputs layer-by-layer up to prediction $y$.
  2. Backward Pass: Calculate output error terms $\delta^{(2)}$, propagate them backward to compute hidden layer error terms $\delta^{(1)}$, and scale by layer inputs to get weight gradients.

While scalar notation makes intermediate dependencies easy to track, vectorized implementations run much faster on hardware. Check out Backpropagation in Matrix Calculus to see how these operations translate directly into matrix multiplications.

Let $w_{ij}^{(2)}$ be the weight connecting hidden unit $h_j$ to output unit $y_i$.

  1. Weighted sum plus bias:
$$z_i^{(2)} = \sum_{j} w_{ij}^{(2)} h_j + b_i^{(2)}$$
  1. Activation function application (e.g., Sigmoid $\sigma$):
$$y_i = \sigma(z_i^{(2)})$$

To find how changes in $w_{ij}^{(2)}$ affect total loss $E$, we decompose $\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}}$ into three partial derivatives:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial y_i} \cdot \frac{\partial y_i}{\partial z_i^{(2)}} \cdot \frac{\partial z_i^{(2)}}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}}$$

Let’s compute each term:

  • Term 1: Derivative of error w.r.t. output prediction
$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial y_i} = (y_i - t_i)$$
  • Term 2: Derivative of activation function w.r.t. weighted sum
$$\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial z_i^{(2)}} = \sigma'(z_i^{(2)})$$

(For the sigmoid function $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, the derivative is $\sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))$).

  • Term 3: Derivative of weighted sum w.r.t. weight
$$\frac{\partial z_i^{(2)}}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}} = h_j$$

Combining these terms:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}} = (y_i - t_i) \cdot \sigma'(z_i^{(2)}) \cdot h_j$$

To simplify notation, define the error term (or local gradient) $\delta_i^{(2)}$ for output node $i$:

$$\delta_i^{(2)} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial z_i^{(2)}} = (y_i - t_i) \sigma'(z_i^{(2)})$$

This lets us express the gradient cleanly as:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}} = \delta_i^{(2)} h_j$$

2. Hidden Layer Weights

Now consider weight $w_{jk}^{(1)}$ in the first layer, connecting input $x_k$ to hidden node $h_j$.

The weighted sum and activation for hidden node $h_j$ are:

$$z_j^{(1)} = \sum_{k} w_{jk}^{(1)} x_k + b_j^{(1)}$$$$h_j = \sigma(z_j^{(1)})$$

Hidden node $h_j$ feeds into all output nodes in the next layer. Therefore, changing $w_{jk}^{(1)}$ alters $h_j$, which propagates through every output node $i$. By the multivariate chain rule, we sum the contributions over all output nodes $i$:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}^{(1)}} = \left( \sum_{i} \frac{\partial E}{\partial z_i^{(2)}} \cdot \frac{\partial z_i^{(2)}}{\partial h_j} \right) \cdot \frac{\partial h_j}{\partial z_j^{(1)}} \cdot \frac{\partial z_j^{(1)}}{\partial w_{jk}^{(1)}}$$

Breaking down these components:

  • From the output layer analysis, $\frac{\partial E}{\partial z_i^{(2)}} = \delta_i^{(2)}$.
  • The derivative of output linear combination w.r.t hidden activation is:
$$\frac{\partial z_i^{(2)}}{\partial h_j} = w_{ij}^{(2)}$$
  • The activation derivative is:
$$\frac{\partial h_j}{\partial z_j^{(1)}} = \sigma'(z_j^{(1)})$$
  • The derivative w.r.t the weight itself is:
$$\frac{\partial z_j^{(1)}}{\partial w_{jk}^{(1)}} = x_k$$

Substituting these back into our expression gives:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}^{(1)}} = \left( \sum_{i} \delta_i^{(2)} w_{ij}^{(2)} \right) \cdot \sigma'(z_j^{(1)}) \cdot x_k$$

Defining the hidden layer error term $\delta_j^{(1)}$:

$$\delta_j^{(1)} = \left( \sum_{i} \delta_i^{(2)} w_{ij}^{(2)} \right) \sigma'(z_j^{(1)})$$

The gradient simplifies to:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}^{(1)}} = \delta_j^{(1)} x_k$$

Notice the pattern: for any weight connecting node $A$ to node $B$, the gradient is equal to the error term $\delta$ at node $B$ multiplied by the activation input from node $A$.

Updating Weights with Gradient Descent

Once gradients are computed for all weights and biases, parameters are updated in the direction opposite to the gradient to minimize total loss $E$:

$$w_{ij}^{(2)} \leftarrow w_{ij}^{(2)} - \eta \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}^{(2)}}$$$$w_{jk}^{(1)} \leftarrow w_{jk}^{(1)} - \eta \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}^{(1)}}$$

Where $\eta > 0$ is the learning rate, controlling the step size of each update. Biases are updated identically using their respective $\delta$ terms:

$$b_i^{(2)} \leftarrow b_i^{(2)} - \eta \, \delta_i^{(2)}$$$$b_j^{(1)} \leftarrow b_j^{(1)} - \eta \, \delta_j^{(1)}$$

Summary

Backpropagation breaks down loss optimization into two steps:

  1. Forward Pass: Compute activation outputs layer-by-layer up to prediction $y$.
  2. Backward Pass: Calculate output error terms $\delta^{(2)}$, propagate them backward to compute hidden layer error terms $\delta^{(1)}$, and scale by layer inputs to get weight gradients.
